speechtext:
that the third report of the special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on divorce, presented to the house on Thursday, November 3, 1966, be concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the motion is to reduce the quorum of the committee to seven. This is required because of the proliferation of committee meetings. The joint committee has been meeting at 3.30 on Tuesdays. As you know, Mr. Speaker, most hon. members like to be in the house prior to the calling of the orders of the day in order to listen to questions, and so on. Immediately thereafter a number of members, who have other things to attend to, such as committee meetings and so on, can attend to them at that time. Under the committee procedure witnesses read their briefs at the beginning of the meetings. I am happy to say that the members of this house are present at committee meetings immediately after orders of the day.
The purpose of the motion is to avoid the waiting to which the witnesses are often subjected. Some of them may have to wait half an hour or an hour before the committee has a quorum permitting it to proceed with its business, and it is for this reason that I am making the motion. I should say, however, that there was not unanimous consent, as there was doubt in some members' minds that this is a proper and essential motion. The principal object of the motion is to reduce our quorum for the commencement of the meeting to enable us to deal effectively and efficiently with the business of the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I regret not to agree once again with my hon. friend from High Park (Mr. Cameron), but I object to a reduction of the committee quorum, as suggested again today.
In my opinion, the real solution as far as attendance of the members and the holding of meetings are concerned does not consist in reducing the number of members for a quorum; on the contrary, every member of parliament should be allowed to be member of a committee if he wants to. When I consider, for instance, in our comer, my colleague, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) and myself, we are not members of any committee at all, and yet we would be delighted to contribute to the work of committees. Every day I attend the meeting of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, and there are many members of the committee who do not attend at all.
The solution would then be to accept as members of a committee those who would like to contribute to the work, those who are interested in the committees, those who want to be well-informed, those who want to help, co-operate and not reduce the quorum. It is a fact that not many members attend the meetings of the committees and the reduction of the quorum will not bring about an increase in the number of members attending.
The solution, once again, would be to allow those who want sincerely to fulfil their duties as members of parliament, as the hon. member for Sherbrooke and myself, to contribute to the work of committees. We attend the meetings without being members. Our names should be placed on the list of members and there would be two more to reach the quorum.
Other solutions are suggested. Some say: let us reduce the quorum. Mr. Speaker, you will agree with me that that is not logical. The committee on finance, trade and economic affairs very seldom starts its meetings with a quorum. The discussions begin and after half an hour, someone says: Now that there is a quorum, we ask you to regularize what took place before. There are enough members then for a quorum.
But there are members who are not accepted as members of committees. The only members of parliament who are members of no committee at all are my colleague, the hon. member for Sherbrooke, and myself. Will someone say that that is protecting minorities?

I hope that the people responsible for this situation, the party whips, will see to its clarification. I have been asking the Liberal party whip for the past three weeks permission to become a member of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. Later,
I am told. It takes three whole weeks to reach a decision. subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN TWELFTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Again we have another committee asking the house to reduce its quorum from 13 to nine. There are 265 members in this house. The committee in question is the committee on transport and communications. The agenda of that committee includes a study of the problems of the national railways and of the problems of Air Canada, as well as consideration of transportation problems in Canada. Now, out of 265 members, not even 13 are available to look into transportation problems in Canada. And when the time comes to be heard here every member rises in turn, asks questions without any knowledge of the matter and makes inquiries, but no one is prepared to go on the committee to consider transportation problems.
Mr. Speaker, it is clearly unthinkable that we should be asked to reduce the quorum from 13 to 9. I am not on this committee, but if they want to appoint me to it, I will go and carry out the work accordingly. I did that for three years; I have been assiduous in attending the sittings of the committee on transport and communications. I have had the opportunity, during the sittings of that committee, one year in particular, to ask questions of, and get information from, Mr. Donald Gordon, president of the Canadian National Railways; another year, I had the opportunity to question and get information from Mr. McGregor, president of Air Canada; I learned what was involved in Canada's transportation problem.
But you cannot even find 13 out of 265 who will go. I, for one, will go, Mr. Speaker. Bring down the quorum to 10 only and I will go, I will be present. But no, we are not appointed committee members. Therefore, I think this is abnormal. It is illogical. I object to the fact that members of the House of Commons do not take enough interest in the nation's business. They are not interested enough in that. They do not attend the sittings and, consequently, we are asked to reduce the quorum. I object to that, Mr. Speaker, and again I ask that this motion be agreed to but on division, which means that I object to it being concurred in.

The government has a majority of members on each committee. Committees consist of about 24 members, and the majority are from the Liberal party. All they have to do to form a quorum is to have their members present.
They are now acknowledging publicly that they are unable to perform the functions of government. This we have seeen for a long time. We have tried to get that fact across to the Canadian people, and perhaps this will be additional information for the public.
In view of the fact that the rules are under temporary experimentation I think we should continue with them, so that the Liberal party may thoroughly understand the mistake they made when they altered the rules two years ago. Let them attend the committees; let them maintain the quorum, just as we ask them to maintain the quorum in the House of Commons, and then everything will go well.
After the experiment has been concluded they may find out that there are too many committees, which I think is the case. They may find out that the quorum should be set at a different figure, which I also think is the case because we used to operate some years ago with a smaller quorum. But we should not look back. We must look ahead. This is the twentieth century and we have to move forward into it. If 1966, in the twentieth century, requires a quorum of 13, let us be modern and have a quorum of 13. For that reason I think we should retain the present position.
If the committees system is going to be pursued in the house, let us maintain the quorum under this experiment, and let us make sure when people are giving evidence before committees that they give all the evidence and not just what ministers want them to give.

speechtext:
I want to thank the hon. member for giving me this opportunity to clarify the situation. The memorial in question was

November 8, 1966
Inquiries of the Ministry erected at the Citadel in Halifax in memory of men in the Canadian forces and merchant seamen who lost their lives at sea. This memorial was erected after the second world war. An earlier memorial had been erected at Point Pleasant Park in Halifax. Shortly after the erection of the new monument it was found that it was discoloring and was badly disfigured, in fact it was shameful to have a monument in such condition in memory of our war dead.
The Commonwealth War Graves Commission tried in every way to restore the memorial, but finally concluded that it was impossible to do so. Furthermore the department then known as the department of northern affairs and national resources requested the removal of the memorial because its weight was causing damage to the underground passages of the Citadel. Through the co-operation of the Point Pleasant Park commissioners a magnificent site has been obtained at Point Pleasant Park for the erection of a new memorial. Of course it will not be the same memorial as the one that is now being removed. It will be a "Cross of Sacrifice", which the Commonwealth War Graves Commission has erected throughout Europe and elsewhere, and the names, in bronze of the seamen who died during the wars will be placed on this memorial. Not only will it contain the names appearing on the first monument from the first and second world wars but also those names which have come to light since.
The reason for the burial at sea of the stones on which the names had been inscribed on the first memorial is that it was felt that these stones or fragments thereof might be misused. Most of them were committed to the deepest part of the Bedford Basin in the last few days, and a ceremony was conducted which was attended by an official of the Department of Veterans Affairs, the flag officer, and a representative of the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, and was directed by both the Roman Catholic and Protestant clergy in honour and memory of the dead.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before I proceed may I do something which perhaps is somewhat unusual in the course of debate. I have taken note of the fact that an hon. member of this house, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, is presently celebrating a very important milestone in his life: today is his birthday. I believe that this event in the life of a gentleman of his stature, who in my estimation has contributed much to Canada and to this parliament, should be noted, so I will accordingly extend to him the best wishes of every member of this house.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
In regard to the debate with which we find ourselves seized, I suppose it would be more appropriate if I were to use the time allotted to me to put forward the plight of Canada's senior citizens and old age pensioners who are in such a critical position of need at this time. If I have sufficient time I will make reference to this situation, and I might say, Mr. Chairman, that it would not be extremely inappropriate to do so during the course of this particular debate. I also regret that the Minister of National Health and Welfare does not want to listen to me, but this is not my fault. I see he has returned now.
Referring back to the 1962-63 session, I find that on October 1, 1962, as reported at page 72 of Hansard, the following remarks were made by the present Prime Minister during the course of the throne speech debate. I should like to call the attention of the house to this intervention of the Prime Minister who was speaking about priorities at that time. He said:
There are two things specifically we can do under conditions of expanding economy, and which a Liberal government will do. The first is health care and the problems of old age-
That problem is as appropriate today, and as applicable to our situation, as it was then.
The second matter I refer to is health care, so long ignored by the government. I suggest that the government, in our present situation,

ought to look at the priorities of business in front of the house, and compare them with what is happening.
On page 73 there is a second quotation. This might be the crux of my contribution with regard to the defence question. I want the minister to listen to these words, because last night he made a reasoned speech and a reasoned appeal in this house, as did the hon. members for Brandon-Souris, Edmonton-Strathcona, Danforth, and, I believe, the hon. member for Queens. We are coming to the point where we are not too far apart in our thinking. At any rate, on October 1, 1962, at page 73 of Hansard the Prime Minister is reported as saying:
What we should have had years ago, and what we fought for in this house, is a defence committee on policy where we could try to find out the principles-
Today we want to know the principles on which the government is acting on defence matters. We are asking no more than that when we ask for this matter to be referred to the defence committee at this juncture. We ask no more than the Prime Minister asked, and what held true then holds true now. What applied then applies now, just as the matter to do with old age pensions, that I mentioned before, should be applicable now.
We want to show why we think this matter ought to be in the hands of the defence committee. I am sure that the minister, his colleagues in cabinet and the Prime Minister will agree with me that the valuable time which has been wasted here could have been better spent in committee. It is suggested on the front page of one of the newspapers that the opposition does not feel it is important to pass interim supply until this whole question has been debated. We have many people who have volunteered to speak on this question, and there is no reason why this matter should not be before the committee. I say that because last evening the defence bill was not mentioned in the items of legislation announced for discussion. Medicare was not mentioned, and neither was the old age pension bill. These matters are more important to the Canadian people than the defence question.
The minister feels that if he can get interim supply through the house quickly, when the unification bill comes before the house he will have an axe over our heads. We shall have no opportunity to get this subject before a committee until second reading is completed, and the minister does not
November 8. 1966

care what happens after that. The minister, I suggest, has used this issue, and his high office in this country, for his own purposes. I am not making a personal attack on the minister, and I would not want him to think I am. But, I think he has carefully planned his strategy, and he plans to use his position in the Liberal party, and his office as Minister of National Defence, for his own purposes. When one examines the publicity he has had, and the coverage he has had in the news media, one realizes what the motive of the minister is. One has only to think of the time allotted to opposition spokesmen, on the program last Sunday night and the time allotted to the presentation of the minister's views, to realize what I mean. The minister's speech last night was a slight elaboration of his article in the Monetary Times, which carried a great big picture of the minister. I do not know who is responsible for this sort of thing, but the minister has a way of organizing these things.
We do not have the same capacity for organizing. Reference has been made to how he carried on in the last election campaign, having senior ministers making election speeches. No wonder the Conservative party could not get any votes out of the service personnel. We had no chance, because service personnel have had a hammer over their heads ever since they joined. Thank goodness I got out, because I might have been in the same position myself. If the shoe were on the other foot and we were doing this, the minister would be screaming blue murder.
I have another picture here that appeared in the front part of another magazine. I think the minister's coverage in the news media serves to corroborate our suspicion with regard to the position, to which he aspires.
Why do we want this matter to be referred at this time to the defence committee? Also, what are the questions that must be answered? The matters to do with technicality of debate, and of dealing with the arguments confronting the house before second reading, were put on record last night by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona. He showed that we could not raise these questions after second reading. Then, we could not call the witnesses that we want to call, that we think should be called, in order to clarify this question for the Canadian people. The longer this debate proceeds, the more the Canadian people will become aware of what the minister is trying to do. That is why we
Interim Supply
believe the defence committee should be convened, namely, to have the questions which have arisen clarified.
The other night the minister said in the house: "Why sure, send this to committee; we will hear all these people." Anybody who knows about these things realizes we cannot do this. It is not within our competence, after the principle of the bill has been established, to call these witnesses. It is the principle that we want clarified. If the top echelons of command have not been able to tell the public why they have either agreed or disagreed with the minister and left the service, I think it is high time we called them. We have friends in high places too, and I am not referring to any one particular person. This whole position is ridiculous.
I have two letters in my hand, and I can show the minister many more like these. One of these-and I shall not mention the name because it is from a friend-explains the feelings of military personnel with regard to the order from National Defence headquarters about communication with the press. The minister has communicated with the press very successfully. As I say, this letter is from a close friend, so I will not use his name because he would get the chop, as the rest of them have. But standing orders have been issued warning personnel not to speak with the news media. In those orders the position of personnel is set out.
Let me refer to another letter dated November 3,1966.
On a point of order, I will remind the hon. gentleman that it is a rule that letters be tabled after they have been referred to.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: But I did not refer to that letter. I was more crafty than the minister thought I was. I said that I had received a letter and I told him, generally, the contents of it.

retired without pension.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
I could table the second letter. The minister said that the vast majority of service personnel agree with the principle of unification. Let me tell him that this letter says no, that the majority of these people do not agree with the minister. This is what the letter says:
As I am sure you are aware, many of us In the navy today are very concerned that unification of the three services will be a very serious mistake.

November 8, 196S
Interim Supply
We also feel that many of the points relevant to the current public debate on the subject are being overlooked.
Several of us got together to organize our own thoughts on the matter and the result is the enclosed paper-the views of seven junior naval officers, and views which are shared by the vast majority of our friends and acquaintances. As you have shown considerable interest in this subject, we thought you might be interested in our point of view.
One or two points may not have been adequately stressed. The seagoing world is a large international brotherhood of naval and merchant mariners-to this band we in the navy fully belong. To this group, uniforms, titles etc. are the outward and visible signs of a common way of life. To this group these things are important. To do away with these things is to destroy our own self respect, and to cause us to lose respect in the eyes of this international group.
We have pointed out the inconsistency between the minister's policy and the present equipment programme. This is not to suggest that this programme should be cancelled. On the contrary, much of this programme is good and is appropriate to the services as they exist today, and for the future as we see it.
You will appreciate that we cannot sign our names to this paper, but we assure you that it is a genuine and honest point of view.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I need not table this because there is no name on it. But the view is there, and this is a genuine letter from the people concerned. Surely, this is a piece of evidence worth considering.
Let me draw the attention of the minister to an article in this morning's Globe and Mail, part of a continuing series by Scott Young. This is all about a Mr. Merritt, a gentleman who received the Victoria Cross in the second world war. The conclusion is as follows:
In short, like almost everyone, he Is for effective integration, but deeply suspicious of total unification. The point he raises about how the defence chiefs of 1964 felt on the matter is one of many questions that should be answered before the Commons defence committee before the legislation is permitted to go to second reading.
That is another piece of evidence. I think the minister is bound to reach the conclusion that it is essential, and that it is his responsibility, to see that this matter goes to the defence committee before second reading.
What will be the result otherwise? If this debate goes beyond the end of this week, we all know the situation which will arise. We know how many civil servants will not receive their pay cheques. We know that contractors will not be paid, and so on. The responsibility is directly on the shoulders of the minister; it does not rest on any other

member of this house. The hon. gentleman will have to clarify this situation with his cabinet colleagues. There is a long list of other legislation we should be dealing with, but the minister, because of the adamant stand he has taken on this particular question, has seen fit to jeopardize the positions of other ministers of the crown who are responsible for valuable pieces of legislation. And he has done this, as I said a moment ago, for his own motives and in the light of his own aspirations.
To return to the defence issue. As I have said, it does not appear to me that the minister's plans are of overriding importance today in the eyes of the government. There is, therefore, sufficient time available for all these matters to be further considered. The defence committee might easily have three or four weeks in which to discuss them. This is a period to which I subscribe and to which I would endeavour to pledge the members of my party. There should be three or four weeks to discuss these matters so that the people who should be called to make the position clear might be heard.
Surely, this would be to the edification of the minister, also? Surely, the hon. gentleman realizes this, unless he has something to fear. If he has, I can only refer once again to Hansard when his leader put the situation clearly. This is what the Prime Minister had to say on February 4, 1963:
There is one way in the field of national defence in which this leadership might have been shown, in which some of this confusion may have been removed, when a decision might have been taken on the basis of the consensus of the House of Commons; that is by setting up a committee of this house on national defence policy.
Now, we have a committee. It is defence policy that we want to discuss. On the occasions to which I have referred, the Prime Minister went so far as to say the committee should have the right to make policy. I wonder why the minister is so concerned today. We are on the seventh or eighth day of debate. Surely, the other business of the country is important to him. Sometimes I wonder what the government expects from this House of Commons. I tell you here and now, Mr. Chairman, that anyone who looks over the number of items dealt with by the house in the course of any given year will find himself convinced that the opposition has deported itself well, properly and justly. Are we asking too much when we say that this matter should be sent to committee? I do not think so, especially when we are in a position today to make a commitment to the minister,
November 8, 1966



that there would be three or four weeks of discussion in which the committee would not be inhibited. The members could meet, maybe a couple of times a day, and we could conclude the sittings in three or four weeks. We would hold, maybe, 15 or 16 meetings. Since his bill is not even one of those mentioned for early consideration, surely the minister could agree to this suggestion from the opposition.
We are not even asking the hon. gentleman to change his mind in regard to this question. We are simply asking for certain clarification to be made with regard to the principle of unification, clarification which has not as yet been put forward either by him or by any other member of the government. Is this too much to expect? I do not think so.
Then, the time would come for the minister to move second reading of his bill. He knows very well that if he gets his bill through the house on second reading, that is the end of the matter. The government could apply closure if the opposition got out of hand. But he cannot apply closure to this debate. I suggest that one of the biggest errors the minister has made so far was to introduce his bill in the middle of an interim supply debate, because the situation has backfired to his disadvantage. It is a more realistic situation today. The minister was endeavouring to persuade the Canadian public that he was right. He intended to ram this program through and show us up. But it has not turned out that way. If the minister will not accede to the one, simple remaining request to account for his actions, and those of his department, to the servicemen of this country, we can assure him he will bear the responsibility for the supply situation next week when the time comes for the payment of government bills.
What are the points which need to be clarified? It is not enough for me to stand here and say "This is the action we should take." What about the attitude of the personnel? I believe I have already shown that the personnel are dissatisfied and that morale is low. We all know this. This is one of the matters which needs clarification. What about the efficient operation of the armed services, the logistics of the organization, the supply situation, the communications situation? How will all this be affected by unification? There are people qualified to give us answers to these questions. Some of them are in the minister's own department. There are other senior officers who obviously disagree with his point of view on some of these subjects.
Interim Supply
Does the hon. gentleman not want us to have the right to hear them? I ask the minister this question: should we not have the right to hear these people? Is Canada not entitled to know what its armed services are to be expected to do in the future? Is their role to be that of a United Nations troop or organization? Has there been any consultation with the United Nations in this regard? If so, Canadian taxpayers have a right to know, because the whole spectrum of defence would then be altered.
I am not saying the minister would be unable to find an area of agreement. But why is he denying us an opportunity to take up this subject in committee and ascertain, on behalf of this house and of this nation, what the situation really implies?
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
With respect to the area of administration, are we not to have the right to call people who are informed, and who dedicated their lives to their country's service? Have we no right to hear these people? Last, but far from least, what about the historical aspect? How did this come about, so far as the minister is concerned? Has he given us all the facts? I don't think he has. This is a completely new perspective. The word flexibility was used in the white paper, but there was no hard and fast line. Why are we having a noose put about our necks now?
There is enough suspicion about what the minister did in that committee to justify a demand at this juncture that he take this question back to the defence committee and have his own good name cleared. I have no personal battle with the minister. I wish him well. We all know what goes on in political life. I do not think there are too many members sitting here who are that naive any more. But that is no reason for the minister to deny us, or any other Canadian citizen, the right to know exactly what the plan is.
Taking it beyond that, Mr. Chairman, having made a proposal to the minister this afternoon on how to relieve the situation, on how to maintain his position and dignity following further discussion in the defence committee, I suggest that he give serious thought to the whole matter so that no more errors will be made with regard to the progress for which we are all hoping.
A few years ago when in opposition the minister was one of the protagonists of the committee system with regard to defence and other matters. Today, all we are asking is that he bear in mind the position that he and

November 8, 1966
Interim Supply
his leader took back in 1963, and the years before that. If he does that, and if all answers are satisfactorily given to us, then he does not have to be concerned about the position of the opposition.
I have already made reference to the number of items on the order paper that we have dealt with during this session. In that respect, we in the official opposition have proved ourselves to be extremely responsible. So, I do not think the minister and the government can point a finger at the opposition when we put forth a request such as I place before them this afternoon. We make this request in all seriousness, with the hope that for the sake of Canada and our armed services, and for the sake of the future defence of this country, the minister will not be adamant in his views on how to deal with the situation.
We know the rules, and we are not going to allow ourselves to be placed in a corner from which we cannot move. We will not allow the minister to do that to us, and he must examine his own attitude in the light of the responsibility that will sit heavily upon his shoulders this week end.
I am not concerned about the position of our friends to the left. As I said, last night the hon. member for Danforth made a very responsible contribution to this debate. Before that time, I was of the opinion that perhaps his party was using us in another area of manouevres. Today, I am not afraid of that. I am not afraid of it anyway, because the decison is not one to be made by them but by the minister. I assure the minister that this debate will conclude if he will accept the very humble and sensible proposal that I place before him this afternoon.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in the few moments that are left to me I wish to deal with the question of old age security. A few weeks ago I spoke on this subject, and I did not correct the Hansard record at that time. I was recorded then as saying that there was $220 million in the federal old age security fund. The actual sum is $320 million, and I hope that figure will be correctly recorded today.
As has been pointed out by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, this amount could be paid out on the basis of $25 a month to every recipient of old age security at this time without one cent of cost to the taxpayer. I want to ask the government, why is it hesitating to do so? Why will the Prime Minister not answer this question? Why will the Minister of National Health and Welfare

not accede to our request in this regard? That minister is another one of the aspirants to the Liberal leadership, and I have no hesitation in saying that the different roads to the top will cause many heads to bump together.
One thing is abundantly clear and that is, although we have been talking about old age security for almost a year, since last January in any event, the government refuses to move. I have previously quoted the Prime Minister as saying in 1963 that there was not enough attention being paid to our old people. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that statement is more appropriate today than it was then.
What is the government going to do? It is going to impose another tax, as well as a means test for old age security recipients, yet there is $320 million presently sitting in the old age security fund. That is a very unfair proposal. When I spoke about this question some weeks ago, I evoked some answer from the Secretary of State for External Affairs who, as I recall, told me that our proposed increase in external aid was going to be $300 million. Our current foreign aid runs somewhere in the neighbourhood of $300 million, and by 1970 the minister said this would be increased to $600 million, reaching over $1 billion in the ensuing ten years.
At that time I said I heartily subscribed to the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I asked about the senior citizens of Canada who are today living on $75 a month? Mr. Chairman, I tell you it is an impossibility for old age pensioners to exist on $75 a month. The Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Prime Minister must accept the responsibility for not giving to these people the money that exists in the old age pension fund, which has been raised through public taxation and which is available for distribution.
I ask, for what are they keeping it? We also know that a sum of money is being collected under the Canada Pension Plan which is far and away in excess of what the government anticipated would be collected-

Mr. Chairman, I have said that the money in the Canada Pension Plan fund is far in excess of what the government anticipated would accrue in the short period of time since the inception of that plan. I know this to be true. In other words, it is a case of over taxation. But now, we have a situation in which, as a result of the high cost of living, which has been created by the government, the government refuses to heed the needs of senior citizens and old age pensioners. When there is such an amount of over taxation going into the Canada Pension Plan fund, this is extremely unjust.
I shall conclude by saying that I hope the government will take cognizance of what I have said on both these matters. Most of all, I hope that in a serious sense the Minister of National Defence will see fit to accept the proposal that I have put before him this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, although I agree, and as the hon. member for Greenwood made clear the other day, our party agrees that it would serve the purposes of parliament, and probably the purposes of the Minister of National Defence, a great deal better if the bill regarding unification were sent to the defence committee, and although I also agree with the words spoken by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce with regard to old age security pensions, it is my intention this afternoon to deal with the question of the Trans-Canada gas pipeline which has been raised by my colleagues on a number of occasions.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I would not rise to take the time of the committee if I were not profoundly convinced that what the government has done with regard to a line through the United States is a serious sell-out of Canada's economic integrity. Indeed, I suggest that this is a rather shameful present to Canada on the eve of her 100th birthday.
The second reason for my taking up the time of the committee is that it seems to me this is another step, of which there have been a number, which indicates very clearly the 23033-612

direction which this government and the party behind it is now going. Again, I am profoundly convinced that this direction will lead to the destruction-I do not think that word is too strong-of Canada's economic independence, Canada's economic integrity and Canada's economic self-reliance, and will make Canada an economic satellite of the United States. If that is the wish of this government, let me say that I do not want it and I am convinced that the majority of Canadian people do not want it, either.
I think the Minister for Energy, Mines and Resources, when he spoke on November 1, made in his speech a very revealing remark. At pages 9386 and 9387 of Hansard for that date the minister is recorded as having said:
I am often asked, with respect to water, in particular, whether I am a nationalist or a contin-entalist. I answer, by a pirouette, perhaps, that I would be a continentalist if it were in the national interest.
I respectfully suggest to him that a pirouette is hardly the dance step he is really doing. I suggest that the step he is taking is a great deal more violent and less attractive than is a pirouette.
It is the internal contradiction in the minister's mind and in the government's mind, and I suggest in the minds of most or almost all of the members opposite, that worries me as a Canadian beyond words adequate of description.
If I remember correctly the hon. minister was a professor of political science at an Ottawa university before he was elected to this house. Having that fact in mind, the evidence that he does not recognize Canada's position, and that to be a continentalist is by definition against the national interest, is something that worries me very much. The proposition that you can be in favour of an independent Canada-in other words, doing things in the national interest if the word "national" has any meaning-and at the same time be a continentalist is precisely the kind of ambivalence, the kind of two-faced political philosophy which has done immense harm to Canada before today and threatens to do even more harm in the future.
We have at this moment the best possible example of how thoroughly wrong and harmful the government's policy on this point is. After the government has made an agreement with the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company, and after the government of Canada has passed the necessary order in council and has

November 8, 1966
Interim Supply
done these things pursuant to an investigation by a Canadian agency, we all sit here in this parliament, including the minister it he were here, with our mouths open waiting for the Federal Power Commission of the United States in Washington to tell us whether what we have already done can in fact be carried out and under what conditions. Does one need any better example than this? Does the minister know how long will be the delay before the Federal Power Commission makes its decision on the application of the Great Lakes Gas Transmission Company? Does anyone here know what changes that commission may make or what demands it may make on the company? What control has the minister, the government or this parliament as to how this thing will in fact be done, even if the Federal Power Commission gives permission for it to be done?
That is the essential fact about which we in this party complain. It is an essential illustration of the fact that we are throwing our independence away. We can assure the delivery of gas to eastern Canada if we build a line within Canada. We do not have to wait until the Federal Power Commission gives us permission to do it and lays down conditions which may be unacceptable. We can assure our export of gas to the United States by making the necessary contracts with United States companies at Emerson or somewhere else. But the minute we permit the kind of thing the government has permitted, we cannot assure anything because the whole line will be under the control and thumb of the Federal Power Commission.
Why and how in God's name this government could possibly change the policy it enunciated so clearly on August 25, 1966 I simply cannot understand. Several members of my party, and particularly my leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, placed the wording of that statement by the government on record. I should like to repeat just one short paragraph of the release by the Prime Minister on the date mentioned. He stated:
The government does not believe it to be in Canada's best interest that the future development of facilities for bringing western Canadian gas to its eastern Canadian markets should be located outside Canadian jurisdiction, and subject to detailed regulation under laws of the United States which are naturally designed to protect the interests of United States citizens.
As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam stated, nothing has happened between August 25 and today to change the force and validity of the words used by the

Prime Minister on that date. No alleged guarantee that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company has given can in any way change the basic proposition that by building the line on United States territory to bring western Canadian gas to eastern Canadian markets it will be located outside Canadian jurisdiction and will be subject to detailed regulation under the laws of the United States.
As I have already indicated, not only will this line be subject to those regulations, it is now subject to them. Everything Canada has done so far still awaits a decision by the Federal Power Commission before it can be put into effect. The decision of that commission may be entirely different from ours and may be entirely changed.
I have tried to study the National Energy Board recommendation in some detail. Like other members of my party, I have consulted some experts and I have read the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Act. I want to say a few words in relation to some of the allegations and arguments that have been made. The first point I want to deal with is the question as to whether or not the building of the line as proposed, and as agreed to by the government, is contrary to the act incorporating Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited.
Chapter 92 of Statutes of Canada 1950-51, and particularly section 6(a), is very clear in its language. Let me paraphrase the introductory portion. It says that the company may, within or outside Canada, construct and do other things with regard to a pipe line, and then it states:
-provided that the main pipe line or lines, either for the transmission and transportation of gas or oil shall be located entirely within Canada-
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I think those words are very clear. They are clear on two points. They are clear, first, that the legislature-in other words this parliament-recognized that there may be more than one main line; the words are "provided that the main pipe line or lines", and so on. This means that parliament recognized that Trans-Canada might have more than one main line. It is clear, second, that if Trans-Canada has more than one main line, the other main line or lines must also be located entirely within Canada.
The way in which the minister and the government are trying to get out of that clear undertaking in the act is to say that the words "main line or lines" in section 6 (a) mean a main line or lines concerned solely with transporting gas from one part of
November 8, 1966



Canada to another part of Canada, and that the moment the line does something else, the moment it also transports gas outside Canada, it ceases to be a main line regardless of its size, capacity or anything else.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that this is a totally unacceptable interpretation of the words in the act. It is a bit of casuistry and is in violation, in my respectful submission, of the very act which this parliament passed. I do not know what a court would do about it, but I know that as far as I am concerned the government is twisting words when it takes out of this proviso the authority to permit Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to build such a line through the United States.
The fact is that the line through the United States will be a 36-inch line; that its capacity will be somewhere around 50 per cent more than the capacity of the present line in northern Ontario; that it will undoubtedly carry more gas than is carried now in the line through northern Ontario, if not in the first or second year, then eventually; and that it is therefore a main line of the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company. I do not see how anyone can look at it in any other way. It is not a branch line; it is not a feeder line; it is not an adjunct of any line: it is a main line and is therefore in direct violation of section 6 (a) of the act incorporating Trans-Canada Pipe Lines.
There is nothing in this section that defines "main pipe line" as a line that is only for the purposes of transmitting gas from one part of Canada to another. There is no such definition in the section or in any other part of the act. I respectfully submit, therefore, that on this point the government is violating the legislation of this parliament. It is another indication as to the direction of, not creeping continentalism as my leader the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam expressed it the other day but, if he will forgive me for referring to it, it is galloping continentalism that this government is engaged in and has been engaged in for some years.
We have made these mistakes over the years in our oil policy, as was indicated the other day, in the auto trade agreement as has now become clear, and in the fact that we have over the years permitted Canadian industry, particularly the manufacturing industry, to become purely a branch plant industry of the United States. We had another example of this some time ago in the American guide lines to branch plants of American corporations in Canada. These were guide 23033-6121
Interim Supply
lines which our federal government did nothing about until one of the ministers of the then Liberal government of Quebec made a fuss about it across Canada.
Surely, we have had enough examples of the terrible actual damage, and even greater damage potentially, that is involved in this constant giving away of Canadian economic independence. If we had any sense of planning, if indeed we had any sense of responsibility to our nation as a nation, we would have planned another Canadian line for the transportation of gas from the western gas fields to eastern Canada a long time ago. We would have insisted that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines began looping its northern line two or three years ago, so that by now the job could have been finished. Instead, we are under the gun, as Trans-Canada Pipe Lines sought to convince the National Energy Board, and therefore they must have the proposed line now. They thought the line could be built faster south of the border.
I am not at all sure of that. I warn the minister that if the Federal Power Commission should take as long as it usually takes on cases as involved as this one, in view of the very widespread opposition from competing companies in the United States, the likelihood is that if we started the northern line today we would finish it before the Great Lakes company gets permission to build the other line, let alone before they are able to finish the other fine.
The basic resource of Canada, gas and its transportation, is now being put in the hands and under the control of the United States. When it is said that we must have some export of gas to the United States, I agree,-if we have a surplus. I am not competent to say whether we have a surplus. The National Energy Board made calculations and decided that we now have, and will probably continue to have, a surplus for the next number of years. I am ready to accept their expert opinion, although I must say that someone I consulted has very great doubts whether that conclusion will be valid for a very long time.
However, Mr. Chairman, if we need to export to the United States and are able to export to that country, let me make clear that my inquiries have persuaded me that there are other ways of doing it. It is a false red herring-if you can use what is in effect a double negative-to say that we are opposing the export of gas when we oppose this particular method of exporting it. It is totally possible to export gas by selling it at the

November 8, 1966
Interim Supply
outlet at Emerson, Manitoba, or by having someone take it in some short, small, inexpensive branch line that could be built lor the purpose.
The fact is, as the National Energy Board points out, that the agreements for the export of gas which Trans-Canada Pipe Lines now have will result in a worsening of Canada's balance of payments position. It will be the kind of export of gas which does precisely the opposite of that which exports are supposed to do. The reason a country like Canada wants to export is to gain foreign currency to be able to offset the cost of its imports. Exports which result in a net loss of foreign currency are surely not the exports that this or any other country in its right senses wants to have.
At page 6-28 and earlier pages of the report of the National Energy Board, the board analyzes the income from the exports on the basis of the contracts which Trans-Canada Pipe Lines has. It analyses the outgo of foreign currency as a result of this particular arrangement and concludes, as will be found at page 6-26, that the cumulative net outflow would be about $133 million over the first 10 years. The board concludes that there would be a net loss in foreign currency, as a result of this arrangement, of an average of $13 million a year. This will surely affect our balance of payments seriously. At page 6-28, after discussing the entire matter, the National Energy Board says this:
On balance, therefore, the foreign exchange implications of the Great Lakes project appear to the board to weigh against the project, constituting a national cost, though not a cost to Trans-Canada.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I am grateful to the board for the addition of the last words "though not a cost to Trans-Canada"; of course it is not. Trans-Canada is interested in this particular Great Lakes project because it will be able to leave the headache of raising the investment money to its subsidiary, precisely 50 per cent of which it owns which does not give it control over the company, and it will get all the profits involved, through its association with producers and others, without having to do the kind of work it would have to do if the line were built in Canada.
In summary, I say that the argument to which the minister alluded in his speech, that this will be a means of exporting gas and that we need exports, is without basis. The fact is that for the first ten years of this proposition there will be a net outflow of currency. The export of gas will not be in

Canada's interest even though it will be in the interests of Trans-Canada.
Now I wish to say a word about the cost differential because I think that some of the things that have been said, and perhaps some which have not been alluded to, should be put on record. I do not claim to have any expertise in the field, but I have looked at the National Energy Board report and have had it analyzed. I would like to make a few brief comments on this subject, keeping in mind the time which I should observe.
My first comment is that at best the National Energy Board shows a cost differential of about 5 per cent. In its report the Board admits that in such calculations there is a 3 to 4 per cent margin of error. My experts tell me that this is an understatement, that the margin of error in forecasts of this type is much more likely to be between 5 and 6 per cent. Therefore, the margin of error by itself is enough to wipe out the alleged differential in cost, because note should be taken of the fact that all the evidence before the National Energy Board was provided by the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company which was seeking to make its case for the southern line. I will speak about this point again. I therefore suggest to you it does not require great logic to see that if a margin of error is likely, it would not be in the direction of the lower cost but in the direction of the higher cost of the northern line.
The fact that all the evidence came from Trans-Canada Pipe Lines is of great significance. As far as I am concerned, it puts all their evidence under suspicion. I do not say this because I think Trans-Canada Pipe Lines is a worse corporation than any other corporation or that the people who prepared the evidence are dishonest. The point I am trying to make is that, as any member in this committee knows, one does not rely for evidence against a case on the person who appears to plead in favour of it. The National Energy Board relied on evidence given by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines against as well as in favour of the application which it put before the board. Anyone looking at the evidence objectively cannot help but decide that he should examine other evidence before accepting the application.
It seems to me, from the short look I gave to the National Energy Board Act, that sufficient authority is given that body to allow it to make an independent feasibility and cost study of the northern line. I hope that in
November 8, 1966

making this criticism I am not hurting anyone's feelings. I believe that the National Energy Board should have made such a study. Several suggestions have been put forward. To rely solely on the evidence of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines was to ensure that the conclusion would be in favour of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines and against any other line.
As my hon. friend suggests, the company did not even have the right length of the northern line on which it based its evidence.
There is another point regarding the evidence on cost which is a little technical but I hope I can make it clear without taking too long. It seems to me extremely important and striking. In calculating the cost of the two lines the National Energy Board rejected the 8 per cent return which Trans-Canada Pipe Lines wanted for a northern line, and made its calculations on the basis of a 7.5 per cent return. That was the return which Trans-Canada Pipe Lines would have had if it built the northern line, and this return of 7.5 per cent is calculated from the first year on. However, in considering the southern line not only did the National Energy Board accept a 6.5 per cent return but it accepted calculations which make the 6.5 per cent applicable only in the fifth year, not in the first year. I was so struck by that fact that I committed it to memory. I do not have to look up the figures.
In the first year the return is .96 or less than 1 per cent. In the second year the return is 4.45, about 4.5 per cent. In the third year it is 5.53, about 5.5 per cent. In the fourth year it is 6.15 per cent, and it is only in the fifth year that it becomes 6.5 per cent. According to the calculations which were made for me by someone who knows a great deal about this matter, this accounts for the entire alleged difference in cost.
I asked this person, who has had years of experience in the entire field of power, to recalculate the estimate giving the northern line a return of .96 the first year, 4.45 the second year, and so on, and 7.5 the fifth year, not 6.5 as was the case with the southern line. The result was that the cost via the northern line would be smaller even over the first five years; and over the total 10 year period with which we are concerned, the difference in cost would be 4.4 per cent in favour of the northern line. As the leader of my party pointed out the other day, the calculations of the National Energy Board showed the difference in cost over the 10 year
Interim Supply
period to be .22 of a cent, or roughly 1.1 per cent against the northern line and in favour of the southern line. However, if you applied the same rates of return in the first four years to the northern line, the difference would be in Canada's favour, that is the difference would be 4.4 per cent in favour of the northern line.
This is the kind of consideration which should be taken into account by the government, by the committee and by the whole country. It is precisely the kind of evidence which Trans-Canada Pipe Lines would be expected to give, and the fact that the National Energy Board accepted it is a disgrace to its work. The fact that the government accepted and acted on this evidence is a betrayal of Canada's economic interests and of its future. The fact is that the alleged difference in cost to eastern Canada is extremely questionable. According to the information I have received it is probably invalid and totally unreliable.
It is important to realize another point made by the National Energy Board namely, that the building of the line in northern Ontario would bring to Canadians over a period of 10 years a total of $700 million if it were a 30 inch line and a total of $1 billion if it were a 36 inch line.
The National Energy Board points out that not only does the construction of the southern line result in a total loss of income to Canadians but also the construction of various installations and the maintenance of the line and its appendages in the future would have given work and income to Canadians for a long time to come.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
It will now go to citizens of another country. I do not begrudge the citizens of another country work and income, but I am sure that they do not want it at the expense of the Canadian people, and certainly we do not. The real issue that this poses-and this is the reason the members of my party have spoken on this matter with such feeling-is whether we are going to permit this government to continue-

Mr. Chairman, I will not be very long because I am on the last point that I intend to make.
As I was saying, the real issue is whether we are going to permit the government and the party behind the government to lead Canada into economic integration with the United States. As if we did not already have enough of this!
In saying this, I would emphasize, as other members have done, that this is not an antiUnited States stand. For the past 99 years we have had good relations with our neighbour, the United States, and we should continue to have good relations with them. But good relations with a big and powerful neighbour do not mean subservience to that neighbour.
The policy that the government is following in this, as in other matters, will make Canada a subservient satellite of the United States of America. Not because the United States wants this, Mr. Chairman. I do not blame corporations for coming into Canada and investing money when there are opportunities for them to do so. They are merely alert and are doing things in their own interests. I do not even blame Trans-Canada Pipe Lines for trying to bring off a deal which will be in the interests of that company. It is not the business of United States or Canadian corporations to look after the national interest; this responsibility belongs to this government and to this parliament.
I do not blame these corporations or people who take advantage of the opportunity, deliberately created and presented to them by the government, to exploit Canada's interests, even though in the long run they are affected so adversely as to put Canadianism totally in doubt. This is the issue that faces us, Mr. Chairman, and faces us in many ways. It faces us in the economic field and in the cultural field. It faces us when we permit private television stations to use as much foreign material as they do instead of promoting Canada's cultural and spiritual wellbeing in some identifiable way. This issue faces us in all areas.
The reason I emphasize this at this time, Mr. Chairman, is that this Trans-Canada Pipe Lines deal is perhaps as outstanding an example of the sell out of Canada's economic integrity to another country as any example could be.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
However, there are other examples. I would briefly remind the members of the committee, if they need reminding, that the hon. member for Davenport was completely and totally rejected not only as to his prescriptions, with some of which I do not agree either, but even as to his anxiety about what is happening to the Canadian economy. He was hardly listened to by the Liberal party in its recent conference.
The Liberal party went further than this. It not merely rejected the hon. member for Davenport's theories, anxieties and concerns about Canada's economic integrity; it immediately thereafter passed a resolution calling for free trade with the United States. This call for free trade was not wide-ranging, embracing all or a good many of our customers. If it were, Mr. Chairman, this party would have been the first to support it. The New Democratic Party is entirely in favour of free trade because we believe that tariffs have always been and always will be a charge on the purchasing power of the people. If such free trade were to be on a wide basis Canada would be able to continue to be a free agent in the matter of trade.
This was not the view of the Liberal party in conference, Mr. Chairman. It passed a resolution calling for free trade with the United States. Then the Caribbean area was added, but with the full knowledge that our trade there is not worth 5 cents compared with our trade with the United States. I am, of course, talking in relative terms; I am not saying that our trade with the Caribbean amounts to 5 cents. The object of adding the Caribbean was to make people believe that they had gone beyond just trade with the United States, but in fact they had not.
I could not bring any better witness as to the folly of the decision which was taken by the Liberal party in conference than the Prime Minister himself, and I should like to quote again an extremely relevant and important statement of his which is reported in the Ottawa Citizen for October 31. He said:
Canada could not seriously contemplate a free trade union with the United States and the Caribbean countries-
I now ask hon. members opposite to listen carefully to the following wise words. If I may just interject a remark, one of the characteristics of the Prime Minister very often is that his words are wise but his actions go precisely in the opposite direction.
November 8, 1966



Having said that we could not contemplate this free trade union, he continued?
-unless the Canadian economy were strong enough and Canadian ownership and control of all our sources of prosperity complete enough to ensure that we could not lose our political independence.
That, of course, is quite right. But what this Trans-Canada Pipe Lines deal does is that it ensures that the ownership and control of our sources of prosperity will be in someody else's hands; that the extent to which they are in somebody else's hands will be increased.
Once we build the line, Mr. Chairman, we are stuck with it. We must pump the gas through it. We cannot turn off the tap at Emerson even if most of it is used for export purposes. If we did that we would really raise an international problem with the United States and the Federal Power Commission, and we would plunge the company concerned into bankruptcy.
I conclude by pleading with the government not to be obstinate over this. They changed their minds once during the period August 25 to October 4 and they can change their mind again. I urge the government to request the National Energy Board to make an independent feasibility and cost study of a northern line so that we can obtain independent evidence as to what this proposal would really mean. I would also urge the government to withdraw from its agreement with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines and not wait for the F.P.C. to destroy it. I ask the government to think again.
If it will not adopt any of these requests, then I urge the government at least to consider insisting that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines starts to loop the northern line in 1967 instead of in 1970. This would mean that the evil effects of the agreement will at least be slightly mitigated with the Canadian line being looped next year instead of in 1970, as provided by the agreement.

Mr. Chairman, I hope that I will be permitted to deviate from the topics which have dominated the present debate, first the question of unification and second the pipe line. I have listened to most of the debate on the question of unification, but unfortunately I have found that this has not really been the topic discussed. Most of the arguments have been devoted to whether or not the minister is arrogant, or to what degree he is arrogant. I would have hoped that in general the merits of unification and
Interim Supply
the pros and cons of the issue could be debated logically, eloquently and objectively in this house so that all of us who have an open mind on the subject could have had some guidelines to follow in arriving at our own decisions.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I shall now add the last words I intend to utter, this afternoon on the subject of unification. I do not think hon. members should carry into action the threats implied, that unless the minister refers this program to a committee before second reading we shall have a repetition of the flag debate. Nobody wants that to happen. I should think many in this chamber are sheepish when they look back at the flag debate, then realize how the new Canadian flag has been accepted by the Canadian Legion and by those people who fought their battle in an objective and progressive manner.
The other subject discussed at some length in this debate has been the pipe line. The hon. member for York South, referring to the pipe line question, said that it is another indication of our willingness to sell our heritage to the United States. I cannot comment adequately on the topic, because I do not know enough about the pipe line. However, I cannot agree with the statement that the Liberal party and its backbenchers have deserted the hon. member for Davenport, the former minister of finance. I should like to place on record that this country, this party, and the backbenchers of the Liberal party owe a tremendous debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Davenport. The hon. member for Davenport had the courage of his convictions by introducing legislation eliminating the possibility of further magazines such as Reader's Digest and Time magazine coming into this country under false pretences. When the hon. member for Davenport was minister of finance he brought to the statute books of Canada legislation making it impossible for chartered banks of this country to fall into foreign hands. He also brought in legislation that prevented the possibility of our insurance companies being dominated by foreign owners. I share, with many other hon. members in all parts of the house, a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Davenport.
You are in a minority in your party.

I may be a minority in my party, but I still feel that we all share the tremendous apprehension of the hon. member

for Davenport of our vulnerability in the field of communications from our friendly neighbours to the south.
