speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I did not participate in this debate to take issue with my hon. friend, who likes to ask questions. I like to answer them, and I shall try to do so at the end of my remarks. My hon. friend is very courteous. I get along very well with him.
I wish, basically, to talk on two topics of interest to me. One concerns the Department of Labour and the other is a personal project that I have sometimes discussed in the house. As a result of the rash of strikes that have occurred recently, a great deal of hon. members' mail at the moment is devoted to labour questions. Many people in my riding, many people in big business and people from across the country, have written offering suggestions as to how parliament can prevent strikes. Some suggestions-and I am sure hon. members are well aware of them-are completely reprehensible. They are that we virtually outlaw strikes; that we remove this tool from labour. Other suggestions recommend compulsory arbitration is the only solution. Some people try to define those areas where they consider the national interest to be more important than that of labour or management. Surprisingly, however, the theme dominating my correspondence is the crying need for more communication between labour and management.
This morning, and this is what prompted my participation this afternoon, a friend in Montreal phoned me, perhaps agitated by the postal situation, wanting to know why the government did not set up a department to encourage some form of continuous communication between management and labour. I pointed out that such a department, or such a branch within the labour department, has existed for 22 years. This is not something this government introduced. It existed when the hon. member for Ontario was minister of labour. As a matter of fact, this branch has

existed for 22 years. Certainly, the idea of managment-labour consultation originated, as many members know, in England, in 1917. J. H. Whitley organized works councils of management and labour to discuss working conditions, and these became known as Whitley councils.
But, Mr. Chairman, labour-management problems have changed. There is an urgency today for a type of continuous consultation. There was a time when the average wage agreement, to use that expression, drawn up between management and labour in this country lasted for one year. In those days, there was a form of continuous consultation between management and labour. Today, many wage agreements are for two to three years. For that reason quite often there is practically no communication for two or three years between labour and management.
The hostility existing between labour and management during the recent longshoremen's strike in Montreal appalled me. Perhaps there was an historical reason for this. Nevertheless, I must point out that between the meetings leading to the wage agreements there was absolutely no communication between the ship owners and the longshoremen. As a matter of fact, the moment the agreements were signed the ship owner in effect, transferred his interest to stevedoring companies. I often wonder why the free collective bargaining process does not take place between the longshoremen and the stevedoring firms rather than between the longshoremen and the ship owners who often are absentee owners.
* (5:10 p.m.)
Labour and management can no longer afford to sit down every two or three years only, to discuss wages and working conditions. New problems have arisen which are beyond the scope of such periodic meetings between labour and management. These are difficulties brought about as a result of technology and automation, and increasing attention will be paid to them as the new department of manpower reaches maturity.
One of the aims of the department of manpower is to increase opportunities for on-the-job training of employees whose working lives have been disrupted by the results of technology, men who are redundant in department A but who well might find employment in department B if they were retrained. One of the aims of the department of manpower will be to make it possible for an employee to be retrained while still in the
November 8, 1966

service of his present employer. I can well understand however labour's mistrust of such a plan if provisions were not made for continuous consultation before this type of training is introduced.
The Department of Labour has set up a branch called, I believe, the labour-management consultation branch-I may not have the correct terminology-headed by Mr. DeWitt, an expert in this field. I have been pleasantly surprised to note that in the last four years there have been no less than 13 labour-management conferences jointly sponsored by the federal government, the provinces and by labour and management across Canada. Six of these conferences have taken place in Alberta, four in Ontario, two in Quebec city and one in Montreal. The most recent took place in Edmonton last week and no fewer than 475 delegates from the greater Edmonton area, representing almost equally employers and employees, met in a two-day seminar to discuss some of the questions which have arisen out of discussions between labour and management groups across the province.
There are a large number of industrial companies in Canada today where provision is made for meetings, on a regular basis, of committees of six, eight, ten or 12 people, half from management and half from labour, to discuss matters of common interest.
The questions discussed at these meetings are not those which would normally be discussed at formal meetings held every two or three years to consider wages and working conditions. They are, for example, such matters as absenteeism. Why should a man with an excellent record of attendance suddenly absent himself from work two or three times a week? The committee tries to find out what is disturbing the employee concerned in an effort to save the man his job and, what is equally important, to save a good man for his employers. Other matters are discussed, such as manpower training, perhaps, or in the case of smaller companies, dwindling profits. Suggestions for increasing production are considered.
Without boring you with the details, Mr. Chairman, let me simply say that these committees have invariably resulted in the betterment of labour-management relations. They have helped to improve the financial picture of the companies concerned and they have worked for the benefits of labour inasmuch as they have provided solutions on a continuing basis to many difficulties which 23033-613
Interim Supply
might otherwise have become the source of tremendous resentment.
Hon. members may say: that is what labour and management do. What does the government do? How does this concern the federal Department of Labour and what is done in the department to encourage action of this kind? Well, right across Canada we have field representatives of the labour-management consultation branch working in cooperation with the provincial departments of labour and other interested organizations to assist in the formation of these committees. We have pre-printed constitutions to suit the needs of companies with, say 10 or 20 employees. We provide free of charge informational literature and posters. At the request of management and labour, we assist in the discussions which take place in the committees. Then, periodically, we evaluate the work of the committees and conduct research with the objective of making them more effective.
I should like, through the medium of this committee, to pay a tribute to this particular branch of the department which, for some unaccountable reason, does not get the publicity it deserves. I mention publicity not to edify the present minister or the Department of Labour but to encourage men like Mr. DeWitt and others to do an even more effective job.
As one who was privileged to attend meetings of such a committee last week in Alberta, may I say how greatly impressed I was by the degree of co-operation shown between the federal and provincial governments in this particular field.
I should like to turn, now, to the consideration of another topic, namely, the question of the Canadian centenary and what this country is doing, or not doing, about commemorating the Fathers of Confederation. It is _ only natural that I should be concerned with one Father of Confederation more than any other, and that one happens to be the great Canadian known as Thomas D'Arcy McGee. My interest in him does not stem from the fact that we can both trace our ancestors to Ireland. Rather, it is because he was one of the greatest forces for the unification of this country. Certainly, his speeches and writing had a tremendous bearing upon the Atlantic provinces, entering Confederation.
I do not wish to bore the committee with a resume of the life history of Thomas D'Arcy McGee. As the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State so well put it on March 7,

November 8, 1966
Interim Supply
1966, Thomas D'Arcy McGee, who was born in Ireland, was a brilliant speaker, a polished writer, a fine poet and a great administrator. As far as I am concerned, he was a distinguished Father of Confederation.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Furthermore, because of United States influence on our mediums of communication, which the hon. member for York South spoke about briefly, because of the fact that our television, radio and news media subject matter usually originates in the United States, the average Canadian citizen, and certainly the average Canadian youngster, is much more familiar with Davey Crockett and the events which led up to the assassination of Abraham Lincoln, then he is with the events which led up to the assassination of Thomas D'Arcy McGee in 1868, just a few hundred feet from the parliament buildings.
Following Thomas D'Arcy McGee's return to Ireland from the United States and then to Montreal, he was sponsored as a parliamentary candidate in a Montreal riding by the St. Patrick's Society, something which was not unusual in those days. He entered parliament as an independent member. I am sorry to say that in a moment of weakness he became a Conservative, and it has taken almost 99 years for us to live down that fact.
But the important thing is that in Canada today the only symbol of recognition of the contribution that Thomas D'Arcy McGee made to this country is a monument on his grave in the Cote des Neiges cemetery in Montreal which, because of the nature of the stone, is now in complete disrepair.
On February 25 of this year the president of the St. Patrick's Society, Kenneth J. McKenna, wrote to John Fisher, the centennial commissioner, and I should like to read a small paragraph from that letter:
The St. Patrick's Society of Montreal, which was instrumental in bringing D'Arcy McGee to Canada in helping to support him here, now finds itself faced with a serious problem. His tomb, in Cote Des Neiges cemetery, which the society has maintained, is in very poor condition. The stone fagade is crumbling, as stone of that type does not normally last more than one hundred years in this climate and we must consider rebuilding it. Emile Brunet, the noted sculptor, has donated his time to a study of the problem and is preparing a plan showing how the tomb could be repaired.
We are afraid, however, that the eventual cost will be far in excess of our limited finances and would appreciate your suggestions as to how federal assistance could be secured to help with the project.
I do not know if there was any reply to this letter, but I asked the Secretary of State
[Mr. Mackasey.l
if we could not assume the cost of the restoration of this monument as a centennial project, which it is calculated would cost approximately $10,000. After paying tribute no McGee in very flowery terms, the parliamentary secretary to the minister suggested I would be very pleased to learn that under a federal-provincial program of per capita grants distributed by the centennial commission, funds were available for carrying out this type of work. However, under this program all requests must first be approved by the provinces.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it is none of the provinces' damned business, that Thomas D'Arcy McGee was not a Quebecker, that he was not an Irishman, that he was a Canadian and a Father of Confederation, and it is the duty of the federal government to look after his tomb. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, I found out when I got this well prepared answer that it should have included the information there was a one year time limit on such requests. A year from 1967 would have been January 1, 1966, yet on March 7 of 1966 the minister and his department suggested I should appeal to the province of Quebec for financial assistance for this project. Needless to say, the provincial authorities assured me that, while they recognized the contribution of McGee to the unity of this country, the time for making such requests had expired.
I then redirected my request to the department of northern affairs in the hope that this type of financial assistance might be found through the branch of that department which maintains historic sites across Canada. I have been the subject of a lot of good natured kidding about this matter, but I feel very deeply about it because one of the problems that faces Canada 100 years after its confederation is our self-consciousness, our inferiority complex, our lack of appreciation and realization of how great Canadian history really is.
One has only to rediscover the exploits of Radisson, La Verendrye, LaSalle, and of other French Canadian explorers, and to reread the discussions which preceded confederation to appreciate the vision of men like D'Arcy McGee, and I regret that there are none of his type preaching unity across our country today.
I am a great believer in Expo. I will not bat an eye if we are going to lose $100 million on that project. But I am more excited about centennial projects than about Expo, because it is through centennial projects that we can leave some lasting monuments of our
November 8, 1968



first century as a nation. I think we need more of those symbols now than at any time in our history, symbols to which we can look back periodically, which may make us feel a little sheepish and small when we argue about petty issues like bilingualism and biculturalism. While we argue about petty issues, men like McGee are buried in cemeteries like Cote des Neiges dependent on private groups to perpetuate their memory. I am told this is true of many Fathers of Confederation.
Amazingly, Mr. Chairman, I have received a lot of correspondence on this subject. Many of the letters are not from people aged 60 to 70, as one would expect, who would be concerned about the Canada which we all love and want to see continue. I have a letter here from one student, and at this point I apologize for not having answered it. His name is John Shiry and his address 28 Plaza Court, Kitchener, Ontario. In his letter he says:
Dear Mr. Mackasey:
It was with a keen interest that I read your remarks in Hansard (March 7) about Thomas D'Arcy McGee. I am one of the fortunate few who have read more than the one line most of our text books meagrely assign to the memory of this great nation-builder . I have read some of McGee's poems and speeches. I have felt the inspiration of his vision for a great nation, and I have felt a deep sorrow that he is not more widely known.
Further on in his letter he says:
It is almost 98 years since the most eloquent advocate of confederation was cut down by an assassin's bullet. The tragedy is that time has made McGee a forgotten man. Every schoolboy should be familiar with that last great plea for unity which McGee delivered that April eve so long ago. It is so relevant today, when our union is being tested, that every Canadian should read it. If a fund can be set up to provide a suitable monument I will take pride in giving, from my limited resources as a university student, to preserve the memory of one of the greatest Canadians of them all, Thomas D Arcy McGee.
I received many such letters, Mr. Chairman, and I also received a very nice letter from the minister of northern affairs pointing out that he had intended to investigate the matter. But I emphasize that our centennial is only six weeks away. However, the minister informed me that this matter will be on the agenda for consideration at a meeting of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board, which advises the minister on matters of historical importance, and which meeting is to be held soon. The minister's letter is marked "personal and confidential", and so I do not want to reveal what it says. But it does point out that it is not the normal practice for the government of Canada,

through the department of northern affairs, to look after this type of project.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I take this opportunity to congratulate the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. I am sure no one would accuse him of being irreverent of our past history or to the Fathers of Confederation. I was aware of the fact that he visited Ireland and took with him a plaque to mark that birth place because of information I received from the historical division of the St. Patrick's society. We are very much aware of that fact. Let me say in all sincerity that the day will come when the great prime ministers of this country, and I include the

November 8, 1966
Interim Supply
right hon. Leader of the Opposition and the present Prime Minister in that category, must be honoured by something that will endure through posterity.
As Canadians, we have an inferiority complex that we should shake as quickly as we can. The best way to fight Americanism is not by becoming isolationists, as many people think, but in revering those things that are truly Canadian.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member indicated that he would answer a question. My question relates to an earlier part of his remarks. Did I understand him to say he thought a monument should be raised to the anti-Americanism of Walter Gordon?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
It was my hope that the hon. member's question would be more objective and to the point. Walter Gordon is not anti-American; he is a pro-Canadian, and there is a fundamental difference. We do not have to erect a monument to things Walter Gordon has done because they appear on our statute books. He protected our field of communication by making it impossible for our daily newspapers to fall into foreign hands. He protected us in the field of finance by making it impossible for banks to fall into foreign hands. He protected us in the field of economics by making it impossible for insurance companies to fall into foreign hands.
I do not know how many people there are who can walk out of this House of Commons and point with justifiable pride to the type of legislation for which Walter Gordon is responsible. For that reason, I will always respect Walter Gordon.

Mr. Chairman, for a few moments I should like to discuss a matter which is not connected with defence or the Trans-Canada pipe line. This matter is closely related to the matter raised by the hon. member for Verdun, the difference being that in respect to my subject matter the government of Canada did suitably recognize the Fathers of Confederation by the construction of a confederation centre in the city of Charlottetown. Unfortunately, not enough money is being supplied to look after the operating expenses of that magnificient cultural centre.
As most hon. members of this committee are probably aware, the memorial foundation responsible for the operation of this centre in Charlottetown is presently faced with a deficit of some $600,000 and is going behind at the rate of $325,000 per year. Let me make it

abundantly clear to members of this committee, in as vehement terms as I can use, that the government of Prince Edward Island does not have the money to pay off this operating deficit and does not have the fiscal capacity to raise that kind of money.
I think these facts can be substantiated by stating that our province is now faced with a direct debt of something over $44 million. This amounts to approximately $407 per capita. Our total debt charge last year, including interest and sinking funds, was $3,600,000, or about 30 per cent of what the government is able to collect through its own taxes and 12 per cent of its total revenue.
Prince Edward Island is already highly dependent on the government of Canada for sufficient money to carry on the operation of its essential services. In the year ended March 31, 1966, just as an indication of how dependent we are, 58.3 per cent of our revenue came from Ottawa. We received 32.7 per cent from taxes, licences and so on which were collected from the taxpayers and 9 per cent from other sources. When you consider our heavy debt, and the large amount of money required to service that debt, it must be clear that our government has not got the money to provide for the operating deficit of this memorial building.
It is my suggestion that we have not got the money, and I maintain that we do not have the fiscal capacity to raise it. We have only 108,000 people in our province and, as members of this committee well know, they are dependent entirely, or almost so, on two basic industries, agriculture and fishing. The average weekly wage in Prince Edward Island is $63.25, which, according to the latest statistics, is the lowest of any province in Canada.
Let me compare the averages. The national average is $93.51. In Nova Scotia the average weekly wage is $74.67; in New Brunswick it is $76.00 and in Newfoundland it is $82.92. It can be recognized that Prince Edward Island, having the lowest national average, is not in a position to collect any more taxes from its people. Consequently, we do not have the fiscal capacity to provide sufficient money for the operating deficit of this centre. It is my suggestion that we should not be expected to finance the entire operation of that confederation memorial building. This building was erected by the Fathers of Confederation Memorial Citizens Foundation on behalf of all the people of Canada to commemorate the
November 8, 1966

Charlottetown conference of 1864. We are happy and proud that the people of Canada saw fit to erect such a magnifieient structure in the city of Charlottetown.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I do not think it should be forgotten that this is a national shrine. While it may be situated in Prince Edward Island, it nevertheless belongs to all the people of Canada. The Prime Minister, at the formal opening of the building by Her Majesty the Queen, stated very emphatically that this was a national memorial which "honours the past, is inspired by the living present and is a not unworthy legacy to future generations of Canadians who take delight and entertainment from it." When the idea of establishing this memorial centre was first announced, the then prime minister said in this house on March 9, 1962, that the federal government would finance one half of the construction cost but not exceeding $2.8 million. All the provinces of Canada very generously agreed to pay 15 cents per capita toward the cost of construction, and the balance of the cost was to be raised by public subscription.
I believe that the cost of the building when completed was in the vicinity of $5,600,000. It is true that our province did not pay the 15 cents per capita, and for this reason the feeling probably exists throughout the country that we got the building for nothing. But that is very far from the truth. As a matter of fact, I believe I can successfully establish that the province of Prince Edward Island paid more toward the cost of construction of this centre than did any of the other provinces of Canada or the federal government.
We were required, for example, to provide the site. To do this, our government had to contribute a whole block of the most valuable land in the city of Charlottetown. I do not know exactly how much that land is worth but, considering present land values in the city I would judge the value of that city block would be at least $500,000. On the land at that time was a three-storey provincial office building of stone construction which housed five departments of government. This building had been remodelled only recently by the government of Prince Edward Island at a cost of several hundred thousand dollars, but it had to be demolished.
On the site there was also a public library and an art gallery. The public library and the art gallery, which was also a permanent type of building, had to be demolished. As a result
Interim Supply
of the compulsory demolition of these two buildings, our government was faced with the problem of constructing a new government office building because space had to be provided for the offices that were vacated. I do not think the total cost of this building can be properly charged to the building of the Fathers of Confederation Memorial Building, but certainly a percentage of the cost can be attributed to this shrine.
The point is that if we had paid 15 cents per capita, as was paid by the other provinces of Canada, on the basis of our population we would have had to pay only approximately $16,000. I estimate that our contribution, by reason of the fact that we contributed the site and had to tear down two excellent buildings in order to construct this centre, was in the order of $3 million. To arrive at this estimate, I am allowing $500,000 for the value of the site, which I suppose is a very conservative estimate, and the value of the two buildings which had to be demolished.
I am pointing this out to make as clear as I can the fact that our province did not get this building for nothing. The largest contribution made on the basis of 15 cents per capita would be made by the province of Ontario, because it has the largest population. I presume that their contribution was based on the 1961 census, which showed that at that time there were living in the province of Ontario 6,236,092 people; therefore on the basis of 15 cents per capita the contribution of that province would be $935,413. The contribution of the government of Canada was $2.8 million, and I suggest that our contribution was very-close to $3 million. Therefore, it is not true to say that Prince Edward Island got this building for nothing.
We lost out on another score. The federal government made available to all the provinces of Canada $2.8 million to assist in the construction of centennial projects. This $2.8 million is the same amount that the federal government granted toward the erection of the memorial building at Charlottetown. All the provinces of Canada except Prince Edward Island were given this $2.8 million. We were denied this grant because the government said, with some justification I admit, that they had already helped to build in our province a memorial to the Fathers of Confederation and we were therefore not entitled to the $2.8 million. But the fact remains that the centre is now faced with an annual operating deficit of $325,000. Each year it is going behind by this amount. All

therefore, plead with the government to be as generous as possible so as to ensure the continued operation of the centre.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Verdun suggested a few minutes ago that he would like to hear someone discuss the principles of unification, integration or amalgamation of the armed forces, and I will attempt to do so in the time that is allotted to me. I am sure that every serving officer now has a dictionary aside from the book on rules and regulations governing the army, because these three words have been used and misused in the last two or three years. The white paper on defence used the word "integration". A few weeks ago the word "unification" was used, and now Bill C-243 uses the word "amalgamation". In fact, one can hardly keep up with the use of these words and I am not sure that their meaning is well understood. I noticed when the minister was introducing the bill he said that the amalgamation will also establish Canada as the unquestionable leader in the field of military organization. I would like to suggest that he misused that word and that he should have said "the unquestioned leader". We can understand why he should be thinking about unquestionable things. He has been so forthcoming lately in the house that he probably considers himself the unquestionable minister.
The principle of integration applied to certain military functions deserves support. It is an intelligent and forward-looking step. I think fault can be found with the former government for not having integrated certain functions of our services. Perhaps if we had done this we would not have given the present minister such a wide field in which to blunder. I do not think there is any doubt that certain fields in service and supply and in research and development should have been integrated. We only need to look at the history of the United States, the British and the German armies during the last war to see what happens when research and development are not integrated. Training can also be largely integrated. Communications and the command function are more difficult to integrate but to a large degree they have a common purpose. Everything that is done in any armed service is done to provide an efficient combat function. The aim of research is to provide an effective combat unit. This is the difficult part of integration. It may be that it is impossible to integrate and that is
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion why thoughtful citizens all over Canada are disturbed and frightened because nobody has convinced them of the fact that we can successfully integrate our combat function.
This is what is causing people such as Colonel Cecil Merritt, V.C., to write letters, and this is what is causing anxiety amongst officers and former servicemen who have formed the Trio Organization. Do not make the mistake of thinking they are a bunch of Colonel Blimps who are only interested in retaining their Scottish kilts or whatever particular uniform they have. They are deeply concerned about the effectiveness of the combat function of the Canadian armed forces after the minister has done his best or his worst to explain it. Their real and honest concern causes them to give up their service careers and to live on reduced pensions, if they have not been fortunate enough to have received the "golden bowler". Their uncertainty is especially acute with regard to the combat function.
Mr. Chairman, I understand some negotiations are going on with regard to a recess between six and seven o'clock. May I call it six o'clock?

The suggestion is acceptable on this side of the house.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Simcoe North.

At six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I was discussing the genuine concern that organizations such as TRIO and others all over the country were showing concerning the combat effectiveness of the Canadian forces and particularly the effect of unification, proceeding at its present rate. The people concerned say that now is the time to pause and consolidate the advances in integration which have been made. They are concerned also about changes which have been made in the services and in supply techniques. They say that we should take a backward look to assess our progress. We should wait until that has been done and then look carefully to see how, when and if integration should proceed farther.
Some will say: "Why pause now?" I think the time to pause and look at things is before damage has been done to the combat effectiveness of our services. Why does one think that damage might be done? Well, so far as it has gone integration up to now has been full of bumbling, bad planning and confusion. One thing badly handled was the early retirement of officers assumed to be unnecessary, the so-called golden bowler program. We had people in the forces anxious to leave and being kept in against their will, and others anxious to stay being forcibly ejected. Some were given a golden bowler they did not want. There was great confusion with medical discharges, and a lot of bitterness resulted.
How many plans have been made and cancelled? Too often in the integration of units and functions orders were given that such and such a plan would be proceeded with and completed in seven days only to have those orders changed and changed again. It seems no one knew what anybody was doing. I impute no motives to this unseemly haste, but I hope, with people all over Canada waiting for political mantles to fall, that the Minister of National Defence was not trying to get into the position of catching a falling mantle if such an occurrence should come about. I know his great dedication to the changing of the services, and I hope he will not discard his portfolio like a toy, once
November 8, 1966

unification is completed, and proceed to urban renewal or whatever he is now starting to be interested in. Whatever the motives behind it we must face, when we talk of integration, the fact that there has been too much quick planning, replanning and more replanning, and that this has caused the services a great deal of uncertainty. It is no use saying, "I hear nothing," or "They are all behind us". The fact is that when people's livelihood is affected they become concerned.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
People who are familiar with this situation should be heard and their opinions should be considered. We should take time, and this is precisely the moment at which we should pause and look again. There are many questions which need to be answered. We should be given a progress report on the effects of integration on the materiel command. What has been the effect on the former air force establishment at Rockcliffe? Have any of the supply services been integrated? Has Rockcliffe materiel command been hamstrung by the lack of trained personnel? These are things we should be told before we approve the minister's bill in principle, not afterwards.
It was drawn to my attention yesterday that the 15 th Regional Ordnance Depot at Lakeview, near Toronto, is to be closed very shortly. The personnel of the depot are learning about this from suppliers; they have no direct information but they are aware something is going to happen to them. How can morale be good when men are faced by this kind of uncertainty?
This is the time to examine and consolidate the gains which have followed integration. The minister says that recruiting has been less successful overall. Figures for the army and air force are good, he says, but those for the navy are down. I suggest that the recruiting situation is much worse than the minister has indicated and that in any case over-all figures are meaningless. Anyone who is familiar with the troop shortages in Italy when Mr. Ralston went out there in 1944 will know how deceptive total figures can be. There were always shortages. Yet a report would say there were always troops available. In fact, they were not available and I suggest that the same situation exists in our services today. In each of the services there is a shortage of key troops and our forces are much less effective in combat than would be indicated by total numbers alone.
Interim Supply
The minister told us we were in a state of prosperity and that recruiting was slower in consequence. I hope he will not be tempted to. say as a corollary that if we experienced a recession we would get the troops we need. I hope he is not like his friend, Mr. Templeton, who on T.V. in Toronto in 1962 hoped for just enough recession to get the Liberals re-elected. I am afraid that even if there were a recession the type of recruits brought in. would not be the type required. We need highly trainable troops.
We shall never be able to compensate these people at rates of pay comparable with civilian rates. Accordingly, the terms and conditions of service must be made sufficiently attractive to induce recruits to take up a military career. It will take more than the-assurances of the minister and his new hierarchy to convince me that these conditions are forthcoming.
Another reason for pausing at this point is. the need to ensure that the pattern of our armed forces is based on our military requirements. The white paper published in 1964 was a remarkable document-one could support almost any case from it because it was full of bland sentences-but it did at least make an attempt to list our military requirements. There was the mobile force, the strike role of the Starfighters, the heavy brigade in Europe and the anti-submarine role of the navy. In the course of our committee hearings we travelled all over the western world. We talked to military experts. We saw our troops and we saw other troops. Some things were very impressive and some-were less impressive.
One thing which impressed me very much, was the peace-keeping role which our troops, were performing in the Congo and in Cyprus. I was much less impressed by the bombing role of the Starfighters because it seemed to me that even in 1964 those aircraft were becoming obsolete. I doubt that there is very much they can do which could not be done a lot more cheaply by an intermediate range ballistic missile. One leading military authority, speaking about our brigade in Europe, said: "You have the best infantrymen in the world stationed in a place where they are-least likely to be used."
One other thing which impressed me was the effectiveness of the anti-submarine role of the Canadian navy-the research and the knowledge required as well as the plain utility of the role in keeping up surveillance of foreign shipping and helping to maintain the-

November 8, 1986
Interim Supply
seas free and open. Now is the time to re-assess the priority of these roles. Perhaps the mobile force should become the most important, with the anti-submarine role a close second. Instead of scrapping the navy in order to keep up the mobile force and the other services perhaps we should be considering the redeployment of our brigade in Europe.
Perhaps it should be given a mobile role in the area which it now occupies so that when our NATO commitment runs out we shall have a mobile brigade ready-formed. Perhaps we should speed up the replacement of our Starfighters by ballistic missiles. This is the time to pause and consider what our military priorities are and how they can be established.
I have not talked with any retired admirals. I do not know any retired admirals. But I do know that I am married to a retired naval lieutenant and I hear every week end when I go home what makes my opinion of the minister seem kindly. This is the ideal time at which to re-assess the situation. If the minister were to do so he might save his bacon, as it were. What has been done so far, if it is properly consolidated and carefully worked out, has, I believe, been reasonably good on the whole. But to take the next step, to tamper with the combat effectiveness of our forces on a basis of pure theory, is dangerous, and we could get into serious trouble.
The other night in Toronto a friend of mine, who is also a friend of the minister and supports the government point of view on this subject, was taking part in a panel program. He cited, as one of the experiences upon which he was basing his opinion, the ideal unification of the Swiss forces into a single force. I hope that there is no portent in that for the Canadian navy because I would not like the same fate to happen to the Canadian navy as happened the Swiss navy.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I am just a retired sergeant but I am not going to enter the debate on national defence this evening. I will confine my remarks to the other theme of the debate, the route of the trans-Canada pipe line from the west to southern Ontario.
When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources tabled the agreement between the government and Trans-Canada on October 28 some comments were made, and I very much like the one made by the Leader of the

Opposition at that time, as recorded at page 9226 of Hansard:
Are Canadian interests being protected? We should not take the say-so of any minister of this government in this regard. Second, what is being done? Will it undermine the future development of western Ontario and northern Ontario? Those are great areas that require and will require an ever-increasing amount of our gas resources.
These are serious matters, and my suggestion is that the government, in the interests of the Canadian people, should make provision whereby this agreement would be submitted to a committee of parliament for examination. We want to know what is in this agreement. Are Canadian interests protected?
That is what I would have expected from the Leader of the Opposition, he being a veteran of the pipe line debate of 1956 and always having shown a great interest in matters affecting the sovereignty of the country. I approve and support what he said at that time, but I am very disappointed at the subsequent performance of his colleagues throughout this debate. None of them who have spoken have supported the position he took on October 28. His position was quite strong and unmistakable, and on the following day, Saturday, October 29, I noticed a headline in the Globe and Mail which read, "Decision On Pipe Line Is Threat to Canada's Independence, Diefenbaker says." If the subject is that important in the mind of the leader of the Progressive Conservative party, surely other members of his party should have supported him. However, the four other members of that party who have spoken on this subject have all supported the government's decision to allow Trans-Canada to build the pipe line through the United States. These were the hon. member for Bow River, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, the hon. member for Calgary South and the hon. member for Winnipeg South.
I am very surprised that others have not spoken on a subject of such national importance. I am particularly surprised that we have not heard from members from southern Ontario. After all, though this subject is of national concern it is primarily of interest to the province of Ontario and the future development of that province. It is particularly important to northern Ontario, but it seems to me that the members from the southern part of that province should have shown some interest in its future development. Yet to my knowledge, and I have checked Hansard, none of them has spoken on this subject.
November 8. 1966

It may be that they were discouraged from speaking in this debate for one reason which I want to stress. On Sunday I was listening to a member of the press gallery speaking on a radio broadcast covering the week's events in parliament, and he said something like this: The occasion of the interim supply debate gave the members of the N.D.P. a chance to indulge in some anti-Americanism on the subject of the pipe line.
Hear, hear.

I hear someone say "hear, hear". I think it is a very unfortunate trend that if one ever wants to speak in favour of Canada and take a pro-Canadian point of view one is labelled anti-American. I was not satisfied with this reporter's remarks and have written to him asking that he kindly define anti-Americanism. Perhaps this is what is discouraging other members of the Conservative party from participating in the debate.
I noticed that during his speech the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said that the New Democrats were allied with the Texas oil and gas men because these particular people, for quite different reasons, are appearing before the Federal Power Commission in Washington opposing the application by Trans-Canada to build a pipe line through the United States. I say that if you think what you are doing is right it does not matter who your allies happen to be, and in supporting the application of Trans-Canada the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is associating with the same people that his leader termed buccaneers ten years ago.
The fact is that there is a great deal of opposition to the application to build the line through the United States. Understandably the people of northern Ontario are very concerned about it. City councils, municipal councils, labour councils, chambers of commerce and people of all political persuasions in that part of Canada are deeply concerned, and I think the rest of us should be concerned too because our interests are affected.
It has been pointed out by previous speakers that if the line were built in Canada through northern Ontario there would be a great multiplying effect from the money spent on its construction and from the money later paid in taxes to the various municipalities. This would contribute to the prosperity of the whole country. It is something we should be concerned about, and people in the
Interim Supply
great manufacturing centre of southern Ontario should be particularly concerned about it.
It is unfortunate, that there is as much regionalism in this country as there is. It is quite natural when you think of the size of the country but nevertheless unfortunate. At the time of the Columbia river debate there was not much interest shown in the house except by members from B.C. and a few from prairie provinces. For the rest of the members it was rather a bore. It may be that our excessive regionalism is making itself felt in the case of this gas pipe line. People think it is a matter only for northern Ontario and therefore they should not concern themselves about it. That is why I am so dissappointed with the performance of the Conservative party.
Like all Canadian youngsters I went to school and read history books. I read all about Macdonald and the national policy, about the building of the railway through Canada in spite of the fact that the country could have been served by a line through the United States. I read about Borden and reciprocity, and even allowing for a certain amount of malarky that appears in our history books there is a great deal of truth in what these people said and accomplished. This country would not be in existence today if these measures had not been taken.
I have read as much as possible on the subject of the route of the proposed gas pipe line and, as has already been pointed out, there remain a number of unanswered questions. We are told that it would be much cheaper to put the line through the United States but we have not been given firm estimates of the cost of putting it through Canada. A pipe line exists through northern Ontario. The basic work has all been done. Property has been purchased. The trenches have been cut and access roads built. Surely if a second line is to be built to serve the needs of southern Ontario, which unquestionably needs the gas, it could follow the same route.
I know that some of the spokesmen for the pipe line company will say that the present northern route is not the one to be followed, that a more southerly route has been mapped out which would involve the company in more pioneering work, in the purchase of right of ways and in the expensive rock mining that has to be done. I have looked at the brochure published by Canadian Lake-head Industrial Commission Incorporated

November 8, 1966
Interim Supply
which shows a route quite a bit south of the existing route, but I think it would be possible for Trans-Canada to build its second line immediately alongside the existing line, with other areas of northern Ontario being served by lateral routes. I would like to know if a thorough survey has been made to ascertain what the actual costs would be. We might find out that the costs would not be very much different from those incurred in going through the United States via Wisconsin, Minnesota and Michigan, and I stress that it would be of great value to Canada if we could follow the route in northern Ontario.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
In the past the United States government or some of its agencies have unintentionally come to the support of Canadian interests. I think of the time two years ago when one United States brewing company was going to purchase Labatt's. The deal was completed and there was no objection from the Canadian government but the anti-trust division of the department of justice in Washington stopped the transaction. I note in the news today that the United States supreme court upheld that decision. One more Canadian enterprise has been saved for Canadians because of the actions of an agency of the United States government.
It seems to me that it would be a very ironic situation if the Federal Power Commission in Washington came to the conclusion that it should not allow Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to follow the United States route. What would the situation be then? It would simply mean that in order to move gas from western Canada to southern Ontario the company would have to decide to build in Canada, presumably by the most economic route. If this company is to fulfil its commitment to the Canadian people it will have to go ahead and do just that.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Why not do that now?

Yes, why should that company not do so now? I suggest there is a real doubt that the Canadian route would be more expensive to construct. We can make a fairly good guess and say that if the company were required to build in Canada it would find it possible to do so at a price perhaps fairly close to that of the route through the United States. I suggest it could do so very soon. The company could get gas to the markets in southern Ontario within a couple of years time if it started construction immediately.
[Mr. Prittie.l
I have followed the career of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources with a great deal of interest. He is a very capable man and has impressed me as having the interest of this country very much at heart. I really cannot believe that he approves of the reversal of the decision first taken by the government. It seems to me there must be a great deal of this story we do not know. I remember the decision that was taken concerning Reader's Digest and Time and the opposition to that decision by a great many members of the Liberal party. I know that the then minister of finance, the hon. member for Davenport, did not agree with it. Something like that must also be behind the reversal in this instance, because otherwise it does not make sense.
Let me refer also to the accusations about anti-Americanism that we quite frequently hear about those who speak along the lines I and my colleagues have spoken. This is an unjustifiable charge. Anyone with any sense knows that our main trading partner is and always will be the United States. There is no question about that fact or the fact that the United States will always have a great influence on this country and will be the source of investment funds. That is true. But there is nothing wrong with advocating that we do what we can ourselves to lessen that influence to a certain extent.
The influence of the United States is being felt all over the world. The people of western Europe, Australia and New Zealand as well as other countries feel this influence and are concerned about it. Recently the West German government took action to make sure that an important industry in that country was not bought by a United States firm. The Australians and New Zealanders are also concerned in this regard, and the Mexicans, the United States southern neighbours, are very much concerned and have taken much stronger action than we have ever taken.
I suggest again, and there is nothing antiAmerican about this, that it is the duty of this parliament and particularly the government of Canada to attempt to retain and keep to itself as much control as possible of the resources of this country. We cannot do that if decisions like this one are taken. A great many things have happened in the past which have lessened Canadian control of the Canadian economy. Though others may not agree, the Columbia river treaty is certainly a prime example. The disappointing legislation we had concerning publications is another
November 8, 1966

example. This kind of thing is happening all the time, and I do not think we should view the question of the route of the gas pipe line as a single isolated incident but rather as a pattern. Canadians have to take a stand and we in this party feel quite certain that those of us who are opposing the decision of the government have the support of a great many people in this country who are not antiAmerican in any way but rather proCanadian. They want to retain control in this country to the greatest possible extent.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to speak on the defence issue as I believe that the ex-service people will adequately cover that subject. In my remarks I propose to try to speak of something that is of interest across this nation.
The lives of the pioneers on this continent were hard and simple. They were farmers and hunters living in isolation in small communities, unconcerned about the outside world. Their existence was free of the many problems facing the people of the 20th century, which in many instances, have been created by the exploitation of succeeding generations.
It has been stated that two grim spectres beckon mankind toward oblivion. One offers instant wholesale death by nuclear means and the other guarantees eventual starvation when human population exceeds food supply. The powers that be in our world of today are struggling in an all-out effort to postpone these evil days. I propose to deal only with food. Man is rapidly changing those once immutable features around him-the soil, atmosphere and waters, even our seas.
The basic conflict is that between the mounting need for food and fibre and the equally urgent need to preserve the quality of our environment. This is the perspective in which to view the continuing debate over the value and hazards of pesticides and drugs. Of course the use of pesticides and drugs is not the only way in which man is not respectful of his environment. The growth of cities, clearing of forests or draining of swamps, the future prospect of weather control, runaway population and the adulteration of food all promise to change this once undisturbed earth irrevocably. Men can no longer approach nature merely to exploit her. They must now learn to manage her wisely. They must decide what kind of environment they really want and what quality of life they desire to lead.
Interim Supply
To talk of pesticides and drugs only in terms of benefits and hazards fails to grapple with the basic question. Men do need to know exactly what these chemicals do and what liabilities their use may incur. But then we must decide whether, where and how to use them to help build the kind of world we want.
To my knowledge the pesticides most widely used are d.d.t. and its breakdown products, aldrin, dieldrin and lindane. In experiments and studies reported to have been carried out by specialists of the University of Miami school of medicine, concentrations of d.d.t. and dieldrin were found in many humans. Traces of pesticides were found in the tissues of stillborn and unborn babies. The greatest concentrations were found in the fat tissue, but the liver, kidney and brain also carried the residue.
At this time I would like to put on record an excerpt from an article that appeared in and Globe and Mail of February 16, 1966 under the heading "Pesticides Held Threat to Unborn". It states:
An expectant mother can poison her unborn child by drinking milk from a cow that has browsed on forage sprayed by some insecticides, an official of national health and welfare department said yesterday.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
Addressing 65 pilots attending an aerial pest control conference sponsored by the Ontario health department, A. B. Swackhammer of the technical advisory unit, food and drug directorate, said careless crop spraying can have far reaching effects.
Chlorinated hydrocarbons used in some pesticides have the longest effects and can be stored in fat deposits and milk in cattle. He said, "Insecticides, coupled with the effect of radioactive fall-out, could produce babies with two heads and six fingers."
A survey of shorthorn cows found a ratio of 30 parts of insecticide to one million parts of milk. An infant child does not have the resistance to insecticides that an adult has, he said. Mr. Swackhammer also said it would be difficult to deny that use of pesticides has caused death in fish and seagull populations. D.d.t. deposits have been found in fish and the situation is of concern to government wildlife and fisheries departments.
It is now evident that with the indiscriminate use of insecticides there is a danger that man eventually would not be able to find relaxation in fishing because the fish would be contaminated; he would not be able to enjoy hunting because the wild fowl and wild animals would be contaminated and the oceans would fail to be a source of protein because even the oceans would be contaminated. One of the means of combating the population explosion was based on the amount of proteins we could extract from the oceans, but now we no longer have the oceans.
Another speaker, Dr. Keith Ronald of the University of Guelph, said insecticides have reached the Antarctic and penguins are being affected. Dr.

November 8, 1966
Interim Supply
Ronald said the Antarctic was once considered the sterile part of the world. "It isn't any more. It is polluted with insecticide."
Dr. Ronald said that the day is coming when insecticides will he sold in the same manner as poisons with purchasers signing a poison register.
Another consideration that should not be overlooked is revealed in a statement by Professor Lamont C. Cole of Cornell University's division of biological sciences. He contended that certain pesticides like d.d.t. which can kill both helpful and harmful species actually "make life easier for the pests." And he followed that thought with the warnings that d.d.t. and other persistent type pesticides carry perhaps the greatest potential long-term hazards to mankind.
United States Secretary of the Interior, Stewart Udall, said in reference to pesticides:
We have strained mind and dollar to bend nature to our satisfaction. Yet we do not know what the effects may be, nor do we anticipate possible consequences. Blithely we carry on our multi-billion dollar programs in the pesticide field with wholly inadequate research. We could be building our own fool's paradise. The day of reckoning may not be tomorrow, but who knows about the day after.
At this time I would like to refer briefly to the case at Grand Forks, B.C., more specifically known as Sunshine Valley, where several farmers had their hogs, cattle and milk declared unfit for food by the federal food and drug directorate. This was the result of contamination caused by aldrin which had been used for the control of wireworm in potato crops. It was found that the effects of this material remained potent for a long period and would kill wireworm nine years after being administered to the ground. The residue of this chemical was passed on to livestock through forage grown on the potato ground years after being treated with aldrin. Much of Sunshine Valley, which is two miles wide by ten miles long, has been rendered useless by contamination. Several farms have had their complete production declared unfit for food. This is a glaring example of permitting a pesticide to be made available before sufficient research work was carried out so that the end results would be known.
In Sweden, Mr. Chairman, plans are being made to cut down the use of insecticides and weed killers to prevent food becoming polluted by chemicals whose long term effects are not known. The Swedish natural sciences research council, which is working on the problem, has called public attention to the lack of knowledge available on what biocides do to human beings and whether they can

produce cancer. For some time Swedish recommendations have discouraged the use of chemicals on food crops for a "safety period" before harvest. The period varies from three to 45 days depending on the chemicals involved. It is calculated to give them time to disperse before the plants are used. The council now is withdrawing spraying. Carrots grown in such soil can contain a higher percentage of diel-drin than the soil surrounding them. Poisons can also enter the human system through eggs. Grain treated with mercury compounds has, when fed to hens, produced eggs containing the same substance. The Swedish government has now forbidden the use of dressed seed as feed for chickens.
I come now to a matter in which I undesirably became involved. I refer to an experience of having our breeding herd of mink exposed to stilbestrol, with disastrous results. Stilbestrol is an artificial female sex hormone; it does not occur in nature. A female sex hormone is a biochemical substance produced by glands within the body. It circulates in the bloodstream and causes female sex characteristics. Stilbestrol cannot be purchased at a drug store without a prescription but pellets of the drug may be obtained readily by farmers at animal feed stores. Stilbestrol is also available in powdered form to facilitate its mixing with animal cereal feed, and is used by farmers and feed lot operators to increase the weight gain in beef cattle. It has also been used in feeding sheep and hogs. Its use for poultry feed has been unlawful for several years.
In our case the stilbestrol entered our mink ration through the cereal which makes up 15 to 20 per cent of the mixture fed to our mink. Of course I should hasten to say we were unaware of its presence. The mink began leaving their feed and this was the first indication that something was wrong. In a few days other symptoms appeared in hundreds of mink. Many had a complete breakdown of the urinary tract from which the most severely affected died. Post-mortems were performed on several animals in the hope that a correct diagnosis could be established.
Dr. Pridham of the University of Guelph recognized immediately the lack of testicle development in the males, which along with other symptoms pointed to sterilization. Stilbestrol was suspected, and after checking all ingredients in the ration chicken waste was blamed. However, Mr. Chairman, when a survey was made of the 15 ranches involved
November 8, 1966

it was found that the source of chicken waste was not common to all and that the only part of the ration with a common source was the cereal. Samples were collected from different ranches and directed to various laboratories for analysis, including the government research station here in Ottawa.
The several samples checked in Ottawa were declared negative for stilbestrol. Two other laboratories came up with positive tests. So as to make a double check on the Ottawa station as to efficiency, a positive sample was presented for checking, and again a negative test was claimed. If we had been dependent upon government employees, compensation to the extent of nearly $750,000 would never have materialized and it would have been "curtains" for some ranches. I trust their technique has been improved so that some dependence may be justified in other important research which they may be called upon to carry out.
In consultation with the company supplying us with the cereal we found they were using the same mixing machinery for both cattle and mink cereal. The cattle ration was supplemented with stilbestrol, and through careless cleaning a trace of the stilbestrol got into the mink cereal when it was prepared. The damage caused by this small amount indicates the potency of stilbestrol. Our experience also proved that there can be an accumulation of the residue in some of the organs of the body.
To further prove my point I point out that the cereal producers through their investigations admitted that our mink had been exposed to the drug daily for six or seven weeks before breaking down physically. However, the process of sterilization began after the first exposure. Mink continued to die six months after exposure. Most of our males were permanently sterilized and only about 25 per cent of the females regained fertility. This information was made known to the agricultural committee in the hope that the chairman in reporting to the House of Commons would recommend legislation prohibiting the use of stilbestrol in the production of food. This course has not been followed and so I feel it is my duty to put this information on the record.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
To further support my belief that stilbestrol in any form is harmful in food production, a very reliable mink rancher near Calgary informed me that he sterilized his
Interim Supply
mink by feeding beef trimmings. This product would include the lips, the cheeks and other head and carcass trimmings. Here again is evidence that the residue from stilbestrol has accumulated in the meat.
Ten milligrams of stilbestrol per day is prescribed for each beef steer. However, recent experiments indicate that faster gains and greater feed savings have resulted when the level of feeding stilbestrol was increased to 20 milligrams during the last three months of the feeding period. There is always the extra hazard created by over-enthusiastic dosage by farmers and feed lot operators on the theory that if a little hormone will do a little good, then twice or, better still, three times as much will be that much better.
Equally harmful is the implantation of the stilbestrol pellet at the base of the ear with a special instrument. Each pellet contains 12 milligrams and two or three pellets are used on each steer, but here again more could be used. They are absorbed over a period of 120 to 180 days. This is a deplorable practice inasmuch as the rate of absorption of stilbestrol is entirely unknown and therefore uncontrolled.
I could quote from several letters I have received from across this nation which support my views and findings, but rather than that I will quote from the official records contained in Hansard and in the proceedings of the standing committee on agriculture, forestry and rural development which met on July 5.
On June 6, 1966 I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare the following question:
Will the Department of National Health and Welfare ban the indiscriminate use of stilbestrol in the feeding of livestock used for food since the United States food and drug administration have recently recognized stilbestrol as a cancer causing agent and, if not, for what reason?
I received the following answer:
The Department of National Health and Welfare has no evidence of the indiscriminate use of stilbestrol in the feeding of livestock. Market surveys of the meat of cattle administered feed containing stilbestrol have been made and no residues of the drug have been found in the edible tissues of the treated cattle.
I will now read from the proceedings of the standing committee on agriculture, forestry and rural development. This is an excerpt from the discussion that took place in that committee. I will start with the question which I asked in the committee and I think

November 8, 1966
Interim Supply
that from it hon. members will be able to get the gist of the discussion. I said:
Mr. Chairman, I have a related question. We have been informed of all the precautions taken in respect of human tolerances of various adulterations. To your knowledge, Dr. Wells, has any product been ordered off the market because of their diverse effects detected by the researchers?
Dr. Wells made this reply:
I could answer part of that question at least. There certainly has been quite large quantities of different products from time to time ordered off the market or ordered destroyed because they contained various chemicals or one or more chemicals In amounts above tolerance.
I followed his answer by this question:
I would like to follow that up with this question. How do you arrive at what is the tolerance level, especially when there is a possibility of an accumulation of such residue to a point of trouble over a period of time?
The chairman then interjected by saying:
Well I take it, Mr. Noble, again this would be a food and drug responsibility so far as that goes.
Dr. Wells then said:
Well, as an example, and I think Mr. Noble is aware of the example, we had a situation not too long ago where our meat inspectors in one plant suspected by post mortem examination of a group of swine that they had been fed diethylstilbestrol which was discussed fully the other day. In this case samples of the swine were held in the plant, samples were taken and the meat inspector's suspicion proved out to be true and, of course, the total group of swine involved were all condemned. This is the way the thing worked.
Mr. Chairman, the answer I received from the Minister of National Health and Welfare was not correct, and the statement made by Dr. Wells to the agricultural committee supports my argument. This difference in the information is understandable when one realizes the very limited research which has been undertaken in the whole field of adulterations of our food.
I think I have proved conclusively that animals exposed to stilbestrol accumulate the residue in various parts of their bodies and that meat from these animals can be a hazard to our health. Humans should not be exposed to this hazard for the purpose of financial gain to a very few people. The information I have reviewed on the dangers of pesticides should not be taken lightly. In fact, these dangers should be considered with much concern. In fairness to all Canadians this government will have to do extensive research to bring out the true facts so that concrete knowledge may form the basis of legislation which in my view is necessary to correct the whole problem of adulterations of food.

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to speak again in the debate on interim supply, but when I came into my office this morning, a telegram from Mr. C. A. Edwards, provisional president of the P.S.A.C., was waiting for me. It was dated November 7 and addressed to Raoul Caouette, instead of Real Caouette, leader of the Creditiste party, House of Commons, Ottawa, Ontario.

Understand that due to debate in house with respect to armed forces unification, interim supply motion has not been passed. As all civil servants will be affected by delay in delivery of cheques, the Public Service Alliance protests most strongly this apparent lack of concern for the welfare of the government's own employees. We request assurance that your party will not delay the passage of the interim supply motion.
C. A. Edwards,
Provisional President, P.S.A.C.

Mr. Chairman, I have great respect for civil servants and labour organizations, but to take the liberty, for instance, of bringing pressure to bear on Canadian legislators, federal members of parliament-by telling them or asking them to give those unions or those employees the assurance:

"That your party will not delay the passage of the interim supply motion."
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)

That is cornering us a bit too much. I know civil servants need their pay, everyone knows it. I also know that the Treasury Board can give instructions tomorrow morning when their offices are open, to distribute the civil servants' cheques. There is no need to hold the sword of Damocles over our heads and say: "If you do not pass interim supply, civil servants will not be paid."
We meet employees in the halls of the parliament buildings who tell us: "It is your doing if we are not paid; the responsibility rests with members of parliament, who hold up interim supply, if we did not get our cheques on the 5th or the 6th, that is the day before yesterday."
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that that is placing hon. members at the mercy of the decision of a few, not civil servants, but the Treasury Board. If the government would say tomorrow: "We are sending out all the civil
November 8, 1966

servants' cheques, would a single bank in Canada refuse to cash them? Everybody knows that eventually in one, two or three days, even if it took 15 days, interim supply will be passed and the cheques will be honoured. The banks will not refuse to cash a federal government's cheque since they always need the parliament and the government to back up, at any time, the loans they grant here and there, either to crown agencies or to private companies.
Mr. Chairman, I do not like people to tell us: "Pass the supply bill, otherwise, you will be responsible if we are not paid. I say that if the civil servants have not yet received their pay, if it is two, three or four days overdue, let the government order that the cheques be sent out. It is the only way. Then, when the interim supply bill is passed, then banks or the Bank of Canada will be reimbursed for the amounts which would have paid the federal civil servants. It is imperative that those civil servants be paid. There is not a shadow of a doubt about that.
For several days, we have heard mostly about the unification of the three armed services: the navy, the air force, the army. It is believed in some quarters that this unification will greatly hurt the Canadian army, that the government is making a mistake by working towards the unification of the three services.
Personally, I admit that there must be in the three services men with great knowledge in military matters, either in the field of aviation, navigation or land warfare. And since we are talking about unification, there is no doubt that heads will roll somewhere. There will not be three admirals or three generals to head that unified army. Two will have to disappear eventually and that will not suit everyone. We all know that.
But when one thinks of Canada, instead of thinking about one's job, when one thinks about the possibility of our having a more efficient army, an army which will give a better performance, an army which will have more cohesion, and an army where expenditures will be better controlled, an army which of course will cost the Canadian people much less to maintain than three different services, it seems to me that it is quite an easy thing to understand, even if some some heads must roll, as I said earlier.
Mr. Chairman, we must consider the benefits which the Canadian people can derive from the unification of the three services.
Interim Supply
I insist on these four points: greater efficiency, better cohesion, better control over expenditures and a substantial saving for Canadians. This is what I see in the proposition for unifying our three armed services.
And when we see members speaking out against the fact that the soldier or the sailor or the airman will be wearing identical' dress while on furlough, I say these people are being childish, Mr. Chairman; this is simply wasting the time of the house. The enlisted men we meet, whether they be with the navy, the air force, or the army, appear to me to be very well dressed, very well sheltered, and very well fed. In fact, not one of them is excessively thin. Even the admirals or the generals seem to be treated quite well, and some of them even receive fairly generous pensions and they are not complaining. Furthermore, they have the right to such pensions granted to them by the authorities or the Canadian government.
Mr. Chairman, I do not see why there is so much opposition from the Conservative members. I understand that they are patted on the back once in a while by certain Canadian ex-servicemen for defending the pseudodemocratic rights of those army people.
Mr. Chairman, I agree in no way with this fight and filibuster in which the Conservatives are presently engaged in connection with this unification plan for the three armed services. Moreover, the bill has not yet been introduced; when it is put before the house, then will be the time to discuss it and we shall see what its implications are and, then, we can discuss the bill. But, at this stage, it cannot be discussed, since we do not even know exactly what it contains. Therefore,-
Have you read the speech made by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois)?
What was that?
The member for Megantic suggests the opposite.
That does not matter to me. As an individual member, are you not free, within your party?
He was speaking on behalf of the party.
Oh. He was speaking on behalf of the party, was he?

Yes.

November 8, 1966
Interim Supply

Well, I speak on behalf of the movement, absolutely.
Mr. Chairman, those were the comments I wanted to make in this house; when the bill is introduced, we will discuss it, it will get the attention it deserves, according to its implications, but I see only political considerations in opposing unification, under the present circumstances. Even if a member of my party chose to oppose unification, on the grounds brought forward by the Conservatives, I would not agree with him, because I feel that the army must be organized as simply as possible, cost as little as possible, for it has been biting off about one fourth of the national budget for many years in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, those are a few comments I wanted to make on this proposed unification of the armed forces.
I would now like to take up another subject or, rather, to come back to a question already discussed in this house, and to which has been referred to quite often, day after day, so to speak, namely the question concerning inflation.
I received, also this morning, an editorial entitled "Quebec Television" from CFCM station, where it is stated that 365,000 television viewers watch its broadcasts daily. Now, the *commentator in question writes, under date October 27:
Is anybody going to give a thought to consumers?
As far as inflation is concerned.
One could wonder. In the last several months, we have known the effects of an inflationary economy and nobody does anything to check it. In the last few weeks, consumers have absorbed price increases In clothing, food, services, etc. Some products rose so much that they are now beyond the purchasing power of thousands of Canadians.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Recently, the price of cigarettes went up, the price of clothes increased by 10 per cent, the price of cars has gone up, and the price of a gallon of gas increased by 2 cents. Yesterday, we had a threat of a 10 per cent tax increase from the federal government which is short of money to meet provincial demands and, today, haircuts cost 25 cents more in the Quebec city area. The prices of butter, milk, bread, meat, etc. have also gone up. Tomorrow, it will be something else.
In spite of appeals to common sense by the Canadian Minister of Finance, in spite of the consumers' protests, such as the boycott of supermarkets by housewives, nothing works. Prices keep on increasing and there is no indication that this upward trend will stop. It seems everybody wants to hit the jackpot, regardless of consequences.
IMr. Regimbal.]
Everyone seems to forget that following price increases, labour unions will in their turn demand wage increases and, in so doing, will contribute to inflation. If a union obtains a 20 per cent increase, the manufacturer, the industry which granted it, will necessarily increase the price of its products and the wheel keeps on turning with increases occurring in other sectors of the economy. There is too much money in circulation.
