That is the statement of the commentator.
Contrary to Mr. Caouette, we feel that the federal, provincial and municipal governments as well as the school boards are mainly responsible for inflation.
Credit has also become much too easy to get. It is possible to buy with a piece of paper, an I.O.U., thus creating money which does not exist.
At last, here is a commentator who recognizes that with an I.O.U. or a piece of paper, it is possible to buy things and thus create money which does not exist. The bankers do not want to admit it yet to the committees where we have been sitting for some time.
The governments themselves spend lavishly and pile up deficits, thus contributing to devaluating the money in circulation. Governments are mainly responsible for inflation, by starting unproductive projects, such as the Grand 'theatre de Quebec, etc.
It is the responsibility of governments to put a stop to inflation. They have created it by putting on the market a large but artificial money supply whose value goes down each time government deficits increase.
The Ministers of Finance are advising the taxpayers, the consumers to live within their means, and they are the first to disregard that advice. It is time for the governments to assume their responsibilities and impose restrictions, otherwise the country's economy will turn into chaos and the consumers, the taxpayers will have to bear the consequences.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, that commentator is telling the truth but he forgets or does not know the other things which he does not mention. For instance, in his press release sent to all the federal members, all the provincial members, the municipal councils, the school boards and practically everywhere in the province of Quebec, he says that the governments alone are mainly responsible for inflation, that the governments should live within their means. But what is the meaning of means and what does this commentator mean by that word? If he is talking about financial means to develop something, build a school, a hospital, a road, to develop a province, a municipality, a school board or Canada as a whole, if he is only talking about financial means, then I will say that the commentator is right, just as some hon. members in this house are right to say the same thing.
November 8, 1968

But if by means we understand the physical means to build a road, a school, a hospital, to develop our natural resources and the men, the technicians, the men capable and trained to develop what we can develop right here, then, Mr. Chairman, I will say that Canada is the wealthiest country in the world, because we have those means. There are enough engineers, enough materials, nothing is lacking. And the federal government, the provincial governments and the authorities, whether municipal administration or school board, are all right in wanting to develop sectors under their jurisdiction.
But only one government can give them the financial means to develop everything they can, that is the federal government. It can do so because it has the means.
The federal government, the Canadian parliament, can legislate on financial matters. The Canadian parliament has all the means at its disposal, because it can legislate on this matter. It can order the Bank of Canada to coin all possible developments and true resources in this country. Only the federal government has the means to do this. The commentator says:
They are the ones who created inflation by putting on the market a large but artificial money supply.
Who has this money supply, Mr. Chairman? Let us consider the various strikes now taking place in all the provinces. There is talk of an impending strike of postal workers, and the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) cannot answer us. The Minister of National Revenue and President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) cannot give us an answer. But what is at stake in this labour conflict, if not money? What do the postal workers really ask for? They want adequate pay, that is all. It is a financial problem. In the gold mines of my region of Malartic-Val d'Or, there is talk of a mid-November strike. What is the reason, what are the motives behind a strike in my region, the region of gold mines? Is it that the miners cannot work? No. Is it that the mine cannot be operated? No. It is a matter of finance. The miners in gold mines are still earning $1.45 an hour, and that, in areas where the cost of living is far higher than in Montreal or in Toronto and other large Canadian cities. Mr. Chairman, $1.45 an hour, you will grant me, is roughly $50 to $55 a week. Now, how can a family of five, six, seven or eight live on $50 to $55 a week in this day and age?
Interim Supply
What does the commentator mean here by an impressive monetary supply which does not serve the worker, nor the farmer, since the farmer complains about not being able to make more than $2,000 to $2,200 a year? And this same farmer has to work 12, 15, at times, 18 hours a day to manage on his farm. The farmer does not earn as much as a city employee, and the latter does not earn enough to make a decent living.
This means that the money supply to which the commentator refers here is not at the disposal of the Canadian people. At the disposal of whom is it, if not at the disposal of those who have created our money supply.
The chartered banks of Canada, those which coin the wealth of our country, those which, this year, will get out of the national budget, $1,215,000,000 in interest only, those are the ones which have our money supply at their disposal, but not the people.
And we still hear some of those commentators tell the taxpayers to tighten their belts, the consumers to try and put a stop to it. However, what solution will they suggest? They will suggest price control, a freeze on salaries, they will suggest anything. But keep your hands off the financial system which is the cause of the evils of our whole society.
Lincoln was right when he said a long time ago that prosperity cannot be achieved if initiative is discouraged.
Now, this system discourages initiative. We hesitate, we are afraid to do anything, we are afraid to take a chance for fear of being taxed more heavily. Prosperity cannot be achieved if initiative is discouraged, you cannot strengthen the weak by weakening the strong. And that is a fact. And even when, one day they cut Samson's hair who was the strongest man at that time, the king did not get any stronger for that. He himself disappeared without getting any strength.
It is impossible to help the poor by destroying the rich, it is not by taking away from those who have that we enrich those who have not. That is not the way to solve problems.
This is so true, Mr. Chairman, that we see people stir up one class of society against the other. We see people appeal to human passion by saying to the poor: If you live in misery, if you are not successful in life, if you cannot make ends meet, it is because

November 8, 1986
Interim Supply
the rich man who lives on top of the mountain is too rich. If you destroyed his castle, if you burnt his cars, if you burnt everything he has, then you would probably be all right, you would have solved your problem.
Mr. Chairman, those things have happened in other countries of the world. But it is not by destroying the castle of the rich man that the hut of the poor was improved, but the rich man could not, live in his castle, for instance, and he was forced to live in a hut among the poor. That might have brought relief to some, but it did not bring any to the poor, because his standard of living did not improve in those countries.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
You get in trouble when you spend more than you earn. That is obvious. It is impossible to establish a lasting security on borrowed money. Everyone knows that. But it is strange, for instance, that the government does not realize that it is impossible to establish a lasting security with borrowed money, and all the money now at the disposal of the federal government is borrowed money, and nothing else.
The provinces are in the same predicament. The school boards, the municipalities are in the same mess, Mr. Chairman. Money is borrowed for administration for periods of 30, 40, 50 years, with the belief that lasting security is established.
Lincoln himself said that it was impossible to establish lasting security with borrowed money. It is impossible to mould character and courage by depriving man of his initiative and independence. It is impossible to help men indefinitely by doing for them what they could and should do for themselves.
We often witness nowadays governments acting as dispensers of public favours, dispensers of blessings to the population, depriving these people of the opportunity to do by themselves and for themselves what they can do. Governments rob men of their initiative. It is impossible to raise the employee by lowering the employer.
When an employer is not liked, he is usually replaced by a government and wherever a government becomes an employer, it is a worse employer than any private employer. It is impossible to help the small people by crushing the big fellows. It is impossible to help the poor by destroying the rich; which means about the same thing.

One may get a diabolical satisfaction out of crushing or cutting down the big fellows, but that does not help the small people. That may cut down the big fellows; if only it improved the lot of the small fellows, if it made him a little bigger, but no, it does not. Then, why always pick on the "haves" to try stirring up the "have nots"?
Our country, Canada, can provide each and every Canadian citizen with the necessities of life without taking anything away from anybody, without taking anything away from the big fellows or the rich; security can be guaranteed to the small fry, to the family of the worker, the farmer, the labourer, the white collar employee. Security with liberty is the birthright of each and every one in a country as rich as ours. But it has to be achieved with our own means, not by means of the dollar sign, but by our physical possibilities and then the dollar sign can be adjusted according to the actual physical means we have at our disposal for developing our country and guaranteeing security with liberty to each and every Canadian.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take the time of the committee for a few minutes this evening. I may say first of all that I do not intend to talk about Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. However, I am a veteran and a wounded veteran but a veteran of the coal mines, having been carried out of them twice in my lifetime as a very young man. After that I spent a great number of months in a hospital bed and a wheel chair, but I have no service record. So, with my vast knowledge of defence matters, I do not intend to speak on national defence either, as the minister will no doubt be pleased to learn.
I should like to discuss some bread and butter issues. I refer to them as such, and in point of fact they really are bread and butter issues. Some months ago I had correspondence with regard to the employment, or lack of employment, in certain areas of Cape Breton Island. I am sure I will be forgiven by the committee if I am parochial, but this is a most important matter.
I was interested in the telegram which was read by the hon. member for Villeneuve urging us to get the interim supply bill passed so that people could get their cheques. Those people are very fortunate. They will get cheques. The people on whose behalf I intend to say a few words tonight will have no cheques forthcoming and no sign of any
November 8, 1966

employment from which to earn cheques. Therefore I have no apologies to make to anyone for taking the time of the committee.
Before I proceed with the substance of my remarks I might say that since this government came to power it seems that their idea has been to do everything possible to reduce employment in the Atlantic provinces and in Nova Scotia in particular. As my hon. friend from Cumberland said last night, when the Grits get in the Atlantic provinces go down. It would appear that this is so.
A few months ago I received a letter from a parish priest in my constituency with reference to employment at the Cape Breton Highlands National Park on Cape Breton Island. I should like to put a portion of this letter on record. It is dated May 12 and reads:
Dear Mr. Muir: I don't know if you will remember me. We met just a few weeks ago at Neil's Harbour.
That is a village a few miles from Ingonish Beach from where this letter came.
To get right to the point, I am writing about the terrible conditions at the national park here as far as hiring and firing the workers is concerned. I know that you are well aware that in the past the manner of treating the workers left much to be desired. God knows that there is lots of work for everyone if only they would do it. The whole thing has come to a head lately and some of the things which have been going on are unbelievable. It is impossible to find out much from the men themselves. Those working are terrified to open their mouths and those trying to get work are afraid to say anything for fear they will lose a chance for work.
It would appear we are back to a police state with regard to work at this park as a result of the injustice there. This clergyman ends by saying:
We would indeed appreciate it if you would see if something could be done to give our people some security instead of hanging around like dogs waiting for the scraps someone might throw to them.
Yours sincerely,
Rev. L. J. O'Keefe, P.P.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I followed this up with the minister's office, but the reply was not at all satisfactory. Later I received a letter from this same clergyman, dated October 10, in which he advised:
We have close to 50 on relief here already and no one seems to have any hopes of work. There was a lay-off at the park just last week.
Further on in the letter he says:
The election last year was the only time they got work, but there's no sign of one this year-
Interim Supply
Following receipt of that letter I brought this matter to the attention of the House of Commons. The minister concerned was not present and my question was replied to very courteously and co-operatively by the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who is like that on most occasions. Certainly the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Transport could take a lesson from him so far as conducting themselves when replying to questions in the house is concerned. He took notice of my question and said he would refer it to the minister concerned.
At that time I mentioned that 50 families were on relief in the small village of Ingonish Beach. Then, on October 19 I brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration but the Speaker ruled my question out of order. I do not know why, because when people are hungry and need employment I should think it would always be in order to raise the matter. I rose on a point of order and finally was allowed to put my question. As recorded at page 8864 the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development replied as follows:
Yesterday the hon. member asked me If I had an answer ready to this question he had asked previously. I told him I did not have it ready yesterday, and I have not got it ready today, but I hope to have it ready soon.
Following this I received another letter, dated October 17, from Rev. O'Keefe who wrote:
Since I wrote to you there have been 34 more men dismissed from their work. You can imagine what that is going to do for morale here.
The worst part of the whole thing seems to be the lack of concern on the part of those who can do something. Your question being publicized has given the men some hope, since someone finally seems to care enough to try to help us get some work.
Thank you again and I hope you will keep after them until we get some help. Work is what we need and there is lots to be done. These handouts of relief and unemployment are the ruination of the people here. They need work to put them on their feet.
God bless you,
Rev. L. J. O'Keefe.
This is a man whom I do not know but, as indicated in his first letter, I met him once. On November 3 I brought the matter to the attention of the Prime Minister. I thought if I continued to climb up the ministerial ladder I

November 8. 1966
Interim Supply
would perhaps get some action. On that occasion the Prime Minister very kindly said, as recorded at page 9475 of Hansard:
One of the first things I did when I came into my office this morning was to make inquiries into this very important matter. The three ministers concerned have been discussing it and I hope one of them will be making a statement very shortly.
I should point out that prior to that last reference, on October 20 I had originally brought the matter to the attention of the Prime Minister who said he would be glad to look into it. It is all very fine to be told that the government is looking into things and that things are under consideration, but this does not provide pay cheques and does not pay for the groceries. I cannot understand why people in this area should be relegated to the rank of peasants just because these great men who sit opposite are not interested in trying to do something to assist people except at election time. Then they have great words on television and radio and wonderful newspaper advertisements saying they have all the answers and are going to do everything that needs to be done.
I think a man like this clergyman should be honoured for the great humane concern he has for the welfare of his people. In another of his letters dated November 1 he said:
I am not sure but I have been told that there are about 90 receiving relief in this area now. This is not counting anyone north of here.
This is in reference to the areas of North Ingonish, Neil's Plarbour, Dingwall, Bay St. Lawrence and other smaller areas, the residents of which sometimes receive employment at the park, although on occasion it depends on who they are and what political colour they may adhere to.
Now I should like to put another letter dated November 1 on the record. It reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Muir:
We wish to write you on behalf of the children of Ingonish Beach consolidated school. The matter of concern is the serious lay-off of men from the Cape Breton Highlands National Park. Cannot something be done?
Most of these men cannot even draw unemployment insurance benefits and must rely only on municipal welfare. This, of course, does not even cover the cost of groceries let alone provide money for winter boots, jackets, other heavy clothing and Christmas gifts. And, also, no man wants to be dependent when he is able to work.
It seems to us that this matter is sufficiently serious to warrant action from the federal government. Conditions certainly cannot be left as they are.

We would indeed appreciate it greatly if you would see that this is, once again, brought to the attention of the government. Surely they cannot refuse recognition a fourth time. Thank you.
That letter is signed by James MacNeil, principal of the Ingonish Beach consolidated school, on behalf of the school teachers and himself.
What does one have to do to get action from this government? The government can certainly remove jobs. I hesitate to hurt the feelings of the Minister of National Defence, but I recall the great assurances he gave us regarding Point Edward naval base, assurances such as he is now giving the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings in regard to H.M.C.S. Cornwallis and in regard to all these other bases. On that occasion through his action and government planning 700, if not more, jobs were removed from that area.
With respect to the restoration project at Fort Louisbourg, the hon. member for Cape Breton South has raised the question time and again about men being laid off there. Only recently, as recorded at page 8724 of Hansard for October 17, the hon. member for Cape Breton South inquired as follows:
I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Will the Prime Minister look into the problem immediately and have it rectified?
The Prime Minister replied, "Yes, Mr. Speaker." The Prime Minister said he was going to have it rectified but it has not been rectified. Men are still being laid off there, and this has happened all down the line.
In the town of North Sydney the famous, or probably I should say infamous, Minister of Transport is making changes there which will remove approximately 700 to 800 permanent jobs, reducing the work force to 150, with respect to the trans-shipment of goods to Newfoundland through the port of North Sydney, and nothing has been done to replace these jobs.
The sad part of it all is that the Minister of National Health and Welfare apparently is not worrying about either the health or welfare of the people of Nova Scotia. He used to be minister of labour. There is an old story in Cape Breton that he was demoted, kicked out of his position as minister of labour and made Minister of National Health and Welfare. The story ran that he could not provide work so surely now he could find welfare for those for whom he could not find work, but apparently he is not in a position to do that either.
November 8, 1966

[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The Minister of National Defence said last night-I do not have his exact words but I scribbled them down-there is great prosperity in this nation and men are leaving the services to participate in this great prosperity. In Inverness and Victoria counties on Cape Breton Island the clergymen have to speak out on behalf of their people because they are confronted with a very serious situation and are not sharing in the prosperity to which the minister referred. People there actually are hungry and have no money to buy groceries. They really have a problem. These clergymen have to look at the problems of the soul and also problems of the stomach. Surely the Minister of National Health and Welfare who sits across the chamber is an understanding gentleman and knows what I am talking about when I refer to the fact that clergymen do have other jobs besides looking after the welfare of the soul.
I mention the situation which exists in Victoria county and I am sure the minister from Nova Scotia must realize the serious situation which exists in areas near the national park, including Ingonish Beach and also the western part of Cape Breton where the balance of the park is located. Perhaps the minister is not strong enough in the government and is not able to persuade the Minister of Finance and some of the other strong men in the cabinet to allocate some money for a winter works program in the area to which I have referred. These men need only check the record to find that the previous administration through the minister of northern affairs was able to spend more money on these park projects than has been spent since. Worth-while projects were carried out by that administration which helped to alleviate the poor economic situation which existed there. Surely when this government can find millions of dollars to spend on everything else it should be able to find some money to spend on these worth-while projects. I have heard it said that by 1970 we will be spending perhaps $1 billion on external aid. I believe that is a good thing, but for heaven's sake let us look after some of the people in Canada, because that is important too.
Within the last 24 hours I have received several telegrams from individuals complaining about the poor economic conditions which exist on Cape Breton Island. Most of these came from individuals who are not residents of the constituency I represent but rather are
Interim Supply
residents of the constituency of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Surely the most partisan individuals who sit on the other side of the chamber will not say that these are political telegrams and that Muir is just making a political speech or that Muir gets nasty when criticizing the government. I would never do that, and anyone who has heard me speak in this house knows that I never become nasty with the government unnecessarily.
Let me read this telegram which refers to the labour and economic conditions in the areas to which I have referred in Inverness county which is represented by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond. That is the same gentleman who is our Minister of National Health and Welfare and I am sure he is worried and concerned not only about these people in his constituency but about those who suffer difficulties throughout the maritimes. Let me put on record the first telegram which reads:
Labour and economy conditions in north Inverness area at present continue to deteriorate. For two weeks or more request have been made for dredging of harbour and construction of loading pier at Cheticamp to provide an outlet for our forest product to the people of north Inverness area. This is now an urgent matter that requires immediate action. May we be advised what action may be expected.
These telegrams were not sent by the chairman of the Conservative party in a particular area. This particular telegram was sent by Most Rev. George Landry, P.P., Rev. Ron Forgeron, Margaree, Rev. E. Gallant, P.P., Cheticamp, Rev. George Arsenault, P.P., St. Joseph Du Moine and Rev. D. F. Roberts, P.P., S.W. Margaree. These people are in close touch with the ordinary individual and are not up in an ivory tower like some of our cabinet members who forget after an election who elected them. These people are faced with the cold hard facts of families with eight, nine, ten and eleven children trying to exist without an income. These people must make some effort to assist these families, and are confronted at times with some cold hard facts.
I am not going to take the time of this committee to read all these telegrams, which are in the same vein, but I should like to place on record the names of the individuals who have signed them and the areas from which they were sent. This telegram is from Amedee Boudreau, president of the Cheticamp Society L'Assomption. The next is signed by Louis Bourgeois, president of the

November 8, 1966
Interim Supply
Cheticamp Co-operative Society. The next is signed by Peter J. Larade of the Cheticamp Board of Trade. I have another signed by Arsene Chiasson, president of the Lemoine Co-operative Society Limited. The next is signed by M. Kelly, president of the Mar-garee volunteer fire department.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
As I have said, I do not wish to take up the time of the committee in this way, but I wish to place on record the names of the people and organizations who sent these telegrams. Perhaps I can just read the names and the areas from which they were sent. They are: Caliste Leblanc, president of Lemoine Society L'Assomption; Elie Joseph Chiasson, president of Grand Etang Agricultural Society; Henry Roach, president of Society L'Assomption, Margaree; Simon Lefort, president of Margaree Co-operative Society Limited; Patrick Thompkins, president of Margaree Credit Union; and Patrick Chiasson, president of the Grand Etang Fishermen Co-operative. I also have telegrams signed by Milton Au-coin, president of the Cheticamp Royal Canadian Legion; Wilfred Boudreau, president of the Cheticamp Knights of Columbus; Edmond Burns, president of the Cheticamp Society, St. Pierre; Simon Boudreau, president of the Cheticamp fire department; Madame Alphonse Chiasson, president of Cheticamp Les Dames de Ste. Anne; Isadore Aucoin, president of the Lemoine Credit Union; Simon Lefort, president of Le Committee de Development, Acadian du Nord, D'lnverness; Victor Deveaux president of the Cheticamp Credit Union, and Peter J. Larade, president of the Cheticamp Board of Trade. If this is not indication enough to the treasury benches that there is something very seriously wrong in the areas to which I have referred, I do not know what is.
All these people want is a job. This government should be able to provide jobs for them in one way or another because time and time again we have heard their brave statements that they have all the answers and the solutions to all problems. Surely, Mr. Chairman, they can find some employment for these people who have communicated with me.
Not only do we have this problem in northern Inverness country and Victoria county in regard to the men who have been displaced at the Point Edward naval base and the men who will be displaced at the North Sydney terminus of Canadian National Railways, but we have the problems presented by the Donald report on coal. This report recommends

to the government the closing of mines. Mr. Donald has said that within a few years he wants to get rid of 6,500 to 7,000 coal miners. No one has said that the government are going to implement the Donald report, but surely they can make a statement in the house so that we will know what will happen to this industry.
Strangely enough on November 5, 1965, one year ago, the minister of labour as he then was, the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond, issued a statement from his office which referred to government policy in regard to the coal mining industry. The statement said that $25 million was to be provided for the coal industry to modernize and rehabilitate it. Not only were these things to be done but a new mine was to be opened in the Lingan area of Glace Bay. This statement was made a few short weeks before an election. Here we are at November 8, 1966, one year since the election, and nothing has been done. The Donald report has also been available for some time. It has not been available to us because members of the house were denied it for many months. The Donald report was dated in May but was brought forward only recently. Although the report has been available to the government for some time there is still no statement on future policy by the government; yet they are the people who had all the answers to the problems of the coal industry.
I can recall when some hon. gentlemen opposite sat on this side of the house. At that time they had great experts on coal mining. I refer to the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Fisheries, for example. It would really amuse hon. members to look back in Hansard and read the wonderful things they had to say in those days about the coal mining industry. We were led to believe they could just snap their fingers and all these problems would be remedied. But they have not done this. When will they do something to fulfil the promises they made to the coal mining industry?
I have not painted a very pretty picture with reference to the unemployment situation in the areas to which I have referred. Surely when the Prime Minister reads my speech in tomorrow's Hansard he will see that something is done to alleviate this problem. The Prime Minister said to the hon. member for Queens a day or so ago that if he had not been in the house he always read Hansard the following day and is well posted on everything that transpires in the house. I
November 8, 1966

hope that, as he said the other day, a statement will be made very shortly in this connection. The Prime Minister has been consulting the ministers concerned, I presume, namely, the Minister of Manpower, the minister from Nova Scotia, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development under whose jurisdiction the parks fall.
I hope that not too many days will go by before the government takes action in allocating moneys for a continuation of the winter works program. I should not say "continuation", Mr. Chairman, because I doubt that there are many people working at the park. There are so many things to be done in this area. When our party formed the government we called for tenders for a golf clubhouse at the park. Tenders were subsequently awarded. When this administration came into power the minister cancelled that project because he felt it was not needed at the time. However, Mr. Chairman, that was a long time ago and no further steps have been taken since on that proposed project.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must interrupt the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria to advise him that the time allotted to him has expired.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Perhaps the committee would allow me just two or three minutes more.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the committee give unanimous consent for the hon. member to continue?
Agreed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
I thank the committee for their indulgence, Mr. Chairman, and I shall not be very much longer. This is one project that the minister could revive. It is a small job but nevertheless any job that provides one, two, half a dozen, 20 or 30 positions is very important. I am sure that the minister, with his knowledge of the parks and what is needed in them and the advice given him by his officials, knows that many developments could take place in the Cape Breton Highlands National Park. Year after year the number of people visiting this park increases by thousands. It is not make-work projects that are needed but work to be carried out for the development of the park, and such work is there to be done.
Interim, Supply
In conclusion may I say once again that I hope the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, who is now in the house and has been out of the house as a result of having to attend to other business, will get cracking with the Prime Minister, the minister from Nova Scotia, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration and do something for the people who have sent me all these telegrams and letters. These people should not have to get down on their knees like the peasants of old and beg to the high and mighty here in Ottawa.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon the hon. member for Grey-Bruce suggested that the subject matter of the armed forces reorganization bill be referred to the standing committee on defence before second reading rather than following the normal procedure. What is the minister trying to hide in this regard? He says he is doing his utmost and wants the bill to proceed in the normal course of events. I say once again that this is not the normal course of events. It is a departure from the normal course of events. The minister says that every country is going to follow us, even the United States, if we give them time. Can we believe him since he has fired everybody who opposes him? He will not let us call as witnesses before the defence committee those people whom he has fired and who disagree with him. This is the whole crux of the problem.
I want both sides of the question brought out. Members who know me realize I am always flexible. I am ready to accept any rational argument in any regard, but I must hear both sides of the argument. This business of hearing only one side and asking members of parliament to accept it is not the normal course of events. It is only right that members of parliament stand and say, let us hear both sides.
It really only became clearly evident to us after Admiral Landymore was fired that there was another side to this whole problem. In this respect I would point out that there is a series of articles appearing in the Globe and Mail by that very distinguished columnist Scott Young. I think it only fair that I quote from the one which appears in today's issue and which indicates that there will be another one following tomorrow. His article is headed "Merritt Versus Hellyer" and it quotes Cecil Merritt, who won the Victoria Cross, as follows:
One of his statements was that he believed Defence Minister Paul Hellyer's plan for unification of the armed forces to be wrong in principle and that ". . . in war ... if you are wrong in principle, you won't find out until you are trapped." . . .
"In my respectful opinion the worst case facing a cabinet and a minister who is planning an organization for the defence of Canada is . . . mobilization for a world war. I believe that unification will break down if put to this strain, and that we will then have to start again, ad hoc ..."
In other words, what he is saying is that it is fine if we can get along with such a force in peacetime but woe betide us if we are faced with a world condition in which Canada as a proud and free nation feels it must contribute to the defence of the free

world. Woe betide those who amalgamate our defence forces and place Canada in an ad hoc position. That is what Lieutenant Colonel Cecil Merritt has suggested in correspondence with the Minister of National Defence. That is what Scott Young wrote in today's Globe and Mail.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I think all Canadians are proud of this country because of the initiative it has taken in approaching world problems at the United Nations. We have gained a degree of respect because we have asserted our independence and sovereignty in our approach to these problems. What will happen if we deplete our armed services by this proposed unification and end up with an ineffective and perhaps insufficient United Nations police force? One can always find respect for Canadians in all countries of the world including Asia, western Europe and even in Poland, Russia and Czechoslovakia. Canadians can feel proud when they wear the insignia of this country which suggests that Canada is independent and not a satellite of the United States.
To back up my suggestion let me remind hon. members of the fact that many people in other countries of the world mistake Canadians for citizens of the United States and when they are corrected they immediately smile because they are pleased to meet Canadians. This is so because we have asserted our sovereignty and independence in respect of how we think every nation represented at the United Nations and other world associations should be treated. We have not been boastful or over-zealous in regard to our dealings with other countries, which has been suggested as being a fault of the United States.
By amalgamating our services we will do away with our navy, and I should like to know who will defend our coastal waters. As a Liberal member said to me the other night, who do we think will shoot at us? But that is not the question. Our coastal waters, including the Arctic ocean, represent over 50 per cent of the coastal waters of the North American continent and these waters are in close proximity to the United States. No one could possibly think that if we do not provide a defence of these coastal waters the United States will not do so.
Let us consider the consequences of such a defence of our coastal waters, and let us not be children in this consideration. This whole area will be defended by the United States if we do not assert our sovereignty, and let us
November 8, 1966

have no doubt about that fact. Canada will then be in the position at the United Nations or at any other world association or organization of a satellite nation of the United States. I suggest no other conclusion can be reached because the United States will defend these waters in order to protect itself. How could we then hold our heads up as an independent people and fight an independent cause for those friends with whom we are associated at these various world bodies?
If we adopt this legislation proposed by the Minister of National Defence we will sacrifice our sovereignty. Let the members on the other side say "oh, oh", but I hope they will eventually think as Canadians and be as proud of Canada as I am. I should like to think that they are prepared to defend Canada.
Hear, hear.

Some hon. member says "hear, hear", but why does the government of which he is a member insist on disbanding our navy and ruining our national defence services? Why does this government pursue this unification bill without first sending it to a committee for consideration after hearing evidence from experts on all sides? The associate minister said in a speech in the House of Commons that he had some doubts about this procedure until he spoke with some experts. I should like to know who those experts were.
Why does the minister insist on destroying our navy and grounding our air force through this unification proposal which will do nothing for the defence of Canada? What effect will this have so far as the nations with which we are friendly are concerned? It will have no other effect than convincing those co-operative nations that we are contributing little to defence forces.
I realize that it is very close to ten o'clock, but before I conclude my remarks I should like to make a plea to the minister to let us examine this whole situation after hearing from expert witnesses. Let us do that before we approve of this bill in principle. Let us do that before this house is asked to vote in this regard. Let us call the expert witnesses and make up our own minds about the advantages or disadvantages of unification. It is now a little after ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman. May I call it ten o'clock?

PUBLIC SERVICE-PROTESTS OVER LEGISLATION RESPECTING RIGHT TO STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 26 last, I directed the following question to the Prime Minister:
Has he received any protests against Bill No. C-170 and does his government intend to amend it in order to make the right to strike less illusory within the public service?
Tonight, I would like to make a few observations before the house is given a substantial answer.
Among the numerous protests against Bill No. C-170 coming from trade unions, I should like to submit the following suggestions:
1.	It is suggested that Bill No. C-170 be amended, taking largely into account the federal legislation on industrial relations as regards collective bargaining, conciliation procedures and resorting to strike. The government would thus show, in a non equivocal way, that it is not afraid to impose on itself, as an employer, the obligations that the employers of enterprises under federal jurisdiction have to fulfil, as the parliament of Canada wills it. It would also be a token of trust toward federal civil servants, who would surely appreciate the fact of being treated like adults.
2.	It is believed that Bill No. C-170 shows unacceptable preference for trade union structures that are extremely rigid, even totalitarian, and that it places the right of association and union freedom in the background. It seems as though Canada were a Unitarian and homogeneous country. It seems the government is creating a negotiation unit system of so-called "national units". Such structures and units could be of a discriminatory nature and constitute a blatant infringement on sound and proper union freedom.
3.	The arbitration system is perfectly understandable for the duration of a collective labour agreement. In other cases, it is felt that the use of arbitration should be voluntary, without imposing any restriction on its application, as does Bill No. C-170. It should be possible to subject to arbitration any work or employment condition, except perhaps conditions of admission to the public service, if parties agree, when collective bargaining has proved unsuccessful. This should also apply to matters referred to in the recommendations

DEBATES	November 8, 1986
of the Freedman report, when parties are unable to agree, especially if matters relating to technology and automation are involved, which could not be foreseen when the collective agreement was entered into.
It is felt that employees' unions should be represented on the Public Service Staff Relations Board and on the Public Service Arbitration Tribunal. Otherwise, this is implying that only non-unionized employees can deal objectively with the work and employment conditions of federal civil servants.
Finally, it is felt that all officials and members of the board and tribunal should be bilingual with due respect and consideration for both nations which almost a century ago joined in building Canada.
It is suggested that it be clearly established that employees of separate employers should in no way be classified under some groups directly responsible to the Treasury Board as negotiating agent on behalf of the federal government.
I wish to point out to the Prime Minister that the government would be well advised not to ignore such suggestions. The grievances submitted by the employees concerned are numerous and the government would make a bad mistake in imposing Bill No. C-170 in its present form.
The following grievances have also been pointed out to us by unions:
1.	The bill is needlessly restrictive and complex and could only create difficulties in the establishment of sound relations between the government of Canada and its employees.
2.	During the first 28 months following the passing of the act, the employees would be prohibited from selecting the bargaining units they want, which constitutes a serious interference with their right of association.
3.	The employee organizations, even before their certification, are obliged to decide how their grievances will be settled, a choice which is then in force for three and a half years, that is subject to restrictive procedures.
4.	The opportunity to submit grievances and follow them up to settlement by arbitration is seriously limited, thus giving the government unilateral control over a variety of matters such as promotions, demotions, transfers, staff reduction and discipline.
5.	Conciliation, arbitration and arbitration procedures are seriously limited and can lead to delays and unavoidable legal interference

Those, Mr. Speaker, are considerations which warrant amendments to Bill No. C-170 on the civil service.

maintopic: TRANSPORT-RESTORATION OF NAVIGABILITY OK GRAND RIVER
TRANSPORT-RESTORATION OF NAVIGABILITY OK GRAND RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, November 7, I asked the following question of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill): Could the minister advise the house whether his department, either alone or in conjunction with the provincial authorities of the province of Ontario, would institute an engineering study of the cost of the restoration of navigability of the lower Grand River between Brantford, Ontario and Lake Erie for recreational and pleasure craft?
I asked this question because of the importance of the Grand River to one of the most heavily populated regions of Canada partly situated in the area which I represent in this house. I have spoken in the house on this very matter on more than one occasion since 1962. In addition, I have communicated with the Minister of Transport several times in respect of this subject, first with the former minister of transport and later with the present minister, but on all occasions as member of parliament for Brantford.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The Grand River, since earliest times, has been a navigable stream as far as Brantford, and considerable sums of money were spent on its development for navigation prior to confederation, Brantford having been in those days one of the chief ports of entry into Canada. In the 1860's, following the advent of the railways, this most beautiful of rivers flowing through a majestic part of Ontario, beloved of those living in its valley, was neglected. In the meantime millions of dollars have been spent by this parliament on the Trent valley canal system and also on the development of the Rideau waterway system.
I am asking that the minister now direct his attention and that of his department to the redevelopment of the lower Grand waterway system, unparallelled in this country and situated in a heavily populated area. Only today it was announced over the C.B.C. that the minister's department, jointly with the provincial authorities of the province of Ontario, will spend a great deal more money than ever before on an engineering survey of the Rideau water system. All I am asking, Mr. Speaker, is that the minister agree that either his department alone or his department in conjunction with the provincial authorities undertake an engineering study of the redevelopment of the Grand. I am asking for this tonight, Mr. Speaker, but the time will come when the minister will be beset with all manner of representations from different bodies toward this end.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
As a conservational project the redevelopment and restoration of the Grand River is absolutely essential to the area I represent. As a source and place of recreation for the inhabitants of the Hamilton area and for the citizens of the great "Golden Horseshoe", as it is called, around Lake Ontario this beautiful stretch of water is of unmatched importance. I therefore plead with the minister, not only on behalf of my own constituents but on behalf of all people in the area of the Grand River, to give immediate attention to its restoration and redevelopment.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon, I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) whether his department had taken a decision on a site for a regional airport in the Chibougamau-Chapais area.
Several months ago, the Minister of Transport requested his engineers to make a survey of the area and to suggest to him the site most appropriate to serve that area now under full development which lacks facilities for fast communication with the outside.
There are many mining prospects in the Chibougamau-Chapais area, in addition to the mines now under development, and there is also a road more than 80 miles long to Albanel lake through a region having numerous mining prospects, which only have to be developed. Many areas also wait for prospectors, but the present airport no longer meets the requirements and the lack of modern communication facilities stifles the development of the area.
The minister knows that an airport in that area is necessary and justified. Furthermore, it would serve not only the mining industry, but also the development of the tourist industry in that beautiful region strewn with lakes where fish are abundant.
During this summer, Mr. Speaker, I visited the Northwest Territories and found that the 
DEBATES	November 8. 1986
slightest community has an airport which is sometimes very modern.
On that point, the Eskimos are better served than our people back home. And it is unthinkable that the present situation should continue in that mining area. I do not say that the Eskimos do not need airports, but we also need to improve our services in that mining region of Chibougamau-Chapais.
I understand that the department is waiting for the two towns in question to come to an agreement. Of course, it is normal, I think, for the authorities of the town of Chapais to ask that the airport be located close to their own town, where they already have a small airport that could be enlarged and paved. If this site is too close to the town, surely there are other appropriate sites.
The authorities of the city of Chibougamau are also requesting the construction of an airport near their city. There too can be found a site which would appear to be suitable: Lake Cache.
There is no scarcity of sites suitable to build an airport in the area.
It is high time the minister took a decision as far as selecting a site for this airport is concerned; it is not up to the mayor of Chibougamau nor the mayor of Chapais to decide upon such a site. They have already made suggestions in this regard and it is up to the government to select the site which appears to be most suitable.
Therefore, so as not to delay the development of the area, the minister should announce the site he has selected, so that construction of this airport can begin as soon as possible.
